summary: Van Gogh painted his own face about 35 times, most of them in Paris, and the Van Gogh Museum said it was practice in portrait painting.
The piece reads those faces skull first, using an open anatomy textbook and the anatomy book Van Gogh bought in 1884, John Marshall's Anatomy for Artists.

RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, photographed five of the faces in one room of the Van Gogh Museum on 21 October 2026: four self-portraits and one portrait by his friend John Peter Russell.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every museum fact, letter quote and anatomy line was checked word for word against the museums' own pages, the scholarly edition of the letters, OpenStax and Marshall's book. Two things are softer: reading the bone through the paint is the piece's own anatomist's reading, since a painting is not an X-ray, and two quotes rest on secondary sources because the originals could not be opened.

could_be_wrong.point: The count of about 35 depends on what you call a self-portrait and on a few pictures whose sitter is disputed. The museum's own pages say "about 35" on one label and "No fewer than 35" in its guide.

could_be_wrong.point: Some colors seen today are not the colors he painted. Red and purple pigments faded in several of these works, so skin tones are a weak guide to his real skin.

could_be_wrong.point: The museum's object data dates the Grey Felt Hat to September to October 1887, while its description places it in the winter of 1887 to 1888, so the piece gives only 1887.

The words on Russell's portrait are read two ways: the museum says analysis showed "Vincent, in friendship" in red over the head, while Galbally in 1976 gave "Vincent Pictor" and "J. P. Russell Paris 1886 Amitie."

Hartrick remembered "a light blue eye," while Van Gogh wrote that his eyes were green. Hartrick's praise of Russell's likeness comes through Galbally's quote, since his 1939 memoir was not read directly.
The small double-titled portrait may show Vincent or Theo. The museum says there is no decisive evidence, and a painted face cannot always show which brother sat for it.
The 2022 X-ray find rests on a news report quoting the National Galleries of Scotland, because the galleries' own page could not be opened.
Reading the brow, orbit, cheekbone and jaw in the paint is the piece's own anatomist's reading of the pictures, not a measurement. A painting is not an X-ray.

glossary.plain: The single bone that forms the forehead. It also forms the upper rim of each eye socket.
Marshall's name for the smooth ridge above each eye socket, larger toward the middle and fading toward the sides. It is the brow ridge you can feel above each eyebrow.
The upper rim of the eye socket, formed by the frontal bone. The bony rim of the socket is thickened to help protect the eye.
The cone-shaped bony socket that holds the eyeball and the muscles that move it. Seven skull bones build its walls.
The cheekbone. It forms much of the outer wall of the orbit. Marshall called it the malar bone.
The lower jaw, and the only bone of the skull that moves.
Color pairs such as red and green, yellow and purple, and blue and orange. Set side by side, they make each other stronger.
A title that names two possible sitters. The Van Gogh Museum calls one small portrait Self-Portrait or Portrait of Theo van Gogh because no decisive evidence settles who sat for it.

safety.note: This piece reads painted faces for bone structure. It makes no medical claim about Van Gogh and gives no medical advice.

ddw-nl-essay-archaeology-status.title: When does a find become a feedstock?

summary: Under the Dutch Heritage Act, every excavated find is meant to be kept, but the inspectorate wrote in 2025 that some finds have always been left behind or thrown away.
EX SITU, at Dutch Design Week 2026, showed nine designer-artists working with deselected finds from South Holland, with finished objects planned for 2027.
The public pages do not say which find went through which deselection stage, who approved it, or where its documentation is kept.
start_here.how_sure_note: The Dutch law, the inspectorate's report, the ministry papers, the depot's loan terms and the project's own pages were read directly, and an independent check on November 2, 2026 verified the essay. The report's survey answers were not validated, and its reuse percentages are rough.

ddw-nl-essay-material-history.title: What does a new material story forget?

summary: A Dutch Design Week 2026 exhibition at the Gasfabriek in Eindhoven marked fifty years of VIBA and said the foundation is ready for a mature bio-logical building culture.
VIBA's own chronology shows a university chair, a national center, ministerial openings and a 1994 expo, followed by a quiet period, money trouble and moves.
The 2026 monitor puts biobased new homes at about 1 percent in 2025, and a new Dutch rule from July 1, 2026 changes how materials are measured.
start_here.how_sure_note: VIBA's history pages, the Dutch government publications, the national materials database and the 2025 decree were read directly, and an independent check on November 2, 2026 verified the essay. VIBA's history is the association's own account, and the sources give no reasons for its quiet periods or moves.

summary: Luca Ortmann's Waiting for the Bus, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, reimagined places to sit or lean at a temporary bus stop.

ddw26-rnc-001-glass-back-brace.title: An anatomist reads a glass spine

summary: Glazier Eline Laauwen made a back brace out of glass for a school brief on flexibility and stagnation, and showed it at Dutch Design Week 2026.
The real vertebral column supports the body, allows its movements and protects the spinal cord, while a rigid brace limits movement on purpose.
Studies show that holding a body part still costs muscle strength, muscle size and bone, and that the loss can take weeks or months to recover.
start_here.how_sure_note: The anatomy comes from open textbooks and is well established. The studies on braces and on holding still are small or rated low certainty, and several were read as abstracts only. Reading the red lines as nerves is this piece's own comparison.

claims.claim: Eline Laauwen made the brace for a school brief on contrasts, and chose flexibility and stagnation.
claims.source: Eline Laauwen, on camera with RN Collins, Oct 17, 2026

claims.claim: Glass takes only recoverable strains of about 0.1 percent and has no plastic deformation.
claims.source: Rui M. Almeida, "Optical and Photonic Glasses, Lecture 8: Mechanical Properties," International Materials Institute, Lehigh University, spring 2005

claims.claim: The vertebral column supports the head, neck and body, allows their movements and protects the spinal cord.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 7.3, "The Vertebral Column."

claims.claim: The column develops as 33 vertebrae, reduced to 24 plus the sacrum and coccyx; the discs make up about 25 percent of body height between the pelvis and the skull base.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 7.3, "The Vertebral Column."

claims.claim: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and one coccygeal.
claims.source: J. T. Kaiser and J. G. Lugo-Pico, "Neuroanatomy, Spinal Nerves," StatPearls, 2023
claims.study: review; summary read via Europe PMC

claims.claim: Rigid braces are designed to provide maximal support and immobilization and restrict movement in multiple planes; across 10 studies with 970 people, braces may help with pain and daily function.
claims.source: M. B. Borg, M. Battaglia, M. Invernizzi and A. Baricich, "Efficacy of different spinal orthoses for pain management, functional improvement, and quality of life in osteoporotic vertebral fractures: a mini review," Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences, 2024

claims.claim: In 1741 Nicolas Andry published L'orthopédie, and a crooked tree from his book became the symbol of many orthopaedic societies.

claims.source: I. Cuyul-Vásquez and others, "Quantifying the Toll of Disuse: A Meta-Analysis of Skeletal Muscle Mass and Strength Loss Following Upper Limb Immobilization," Journal of Clinical Medicine, 2025

glossary.plain: A maker who works in glass, making objects such as vases, bowls, leaded windows and panels, and restoring old leaded windows.
Permanent bending of a material. Glass has none: it springs back a tiny amount, then breaks.
The flexible column that supports the head, neck and body, allows their movements and protects the spinal cord.
The pad between two vertebrae, with a tough, fibrous outer layer called the anulus fibrosus around a softer, gel-like center called the nucleus pulposus.
One of 31 nerves named for the level of the spinal cord where it emerges, carrying signals both in and out.
The gap between two neighboring vertebrae through which a spinal nerve leaves the column.
An externally applied device used to make up for impairments of the structure and function of the nerve, muscle and bone systems.

ddw26-rnc-002-queer-anatomy-theater.title: Anatomy class, but the microbes are made of clay

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Kuang-Yi Ku tested Queer Anatomy Theater, four hands-on anatomy lessons shown as a work in progress.
The lessons answer anatomy textbooks that studies find picture mostly male bodies and a strict sex binary.
Studies of clay find short-term gains in anatomy knowledge, while the evidence for long-term gains and for augmented reality is thinner.
start_here.how_sure_note: The lessons are described from the press kit and RN Collins's own photos. The teaching studies are mostly small, several were read only as abstracts, and the results on clay and augmented reality are mixed.

claims.claim: Kuang-Yi Ku worked as a dentist from 2009 to 2015, then took a master's in Social Design at Design Academy Eindhoven in 2018.

claims.claim: A 2017 study of 6,044 images from 17 anatomy textbooks found them predominantly male outside sex-specific sections, with almost complete adherence to a sex/gender binary.
claims.source: R. Parker, T. Larkin and J. Cockburn, "A visual analysis of gender bias in contemporary anatomy textbooks," Social Science and Medicine, 2017
claims.study: image analysis of 17 textbooks; abstract read

claims.claim: Among 456 anatomy students, gender-biased images raised scores on a test of implicit gender bias but had no clear effect on stated beliefs.
claims.source: R. B. Parker, T. Larkin and J. Cockburn, "Gender Bias in Medical Images Affects Students' Implicit but not Explicit Gender Attitudes," AERA Open, 2018
claims.study: randomized study of 456 students; abstract read

claims.claim: In German anatomy books, women made up 30 percent of the figures; on e-learning platforms the share reached 66 percent.

claims.claim: Deans in the United States and Canada reported a median of 5 hours of LGBT-related teaching in 2009 and 2010, and 11 hours in 2021 and 2022.

Streed and others, "Sexual and gender minority content in undergraduate medical education in the United States and Canada: current state and changes since 2011," BMC Medical Education, 2024

claims.claim: Students who watched a clay exercise live gained more than the students who did the modeling.

ddw26-rnc-003-walk-through-a-colon.title: What a colon actually looks like, versus the art

summary: Atelier Van Lieshout's Colonic Cleansing Clinic, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, is a walk-in sculpture of the gut that the studio calls deliberately speculative.
The real large intestine is about half as long as the small intestine but much wider, and it holds most of the body's bacteria.
Reviews found no rigorous trials showing that colon cleansing helps general health, and they found real harms.
start_here.how_sure_note: The anatomy comes from a standard textbook, though the same chapter gives two different length ratios. The case against cleansing rests on one systematic review, read as an abstract, a government summary and case reports, so how often harm happens is not known.

claims.claim: The programme describes the clinic as "a functional sculpture shaped like the human gut" and says "The project is deliberately speculative."
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Colonic Cleansing Clinic," programme page

claims.claim: The small intestine is about 3.05 meters long in a living person, and the large intestine is about one-half as long.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 23.5, "The Small and Large Intestines"

claims.claim: The small intestine is about 2.54 centimeters across and the large intestine about 7.62 centimeters.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 23.5, "The Small and Large Intestines"

claims.claim: The rectum is on average about 12 to 15 cm long in an adult.
claims.source: N. K. Santucci, B. Velez, R. Wyllie and J. S. Hyams, "Physiology of lower gastrointestinal tract," Alimentary Pharmacology and Therapeutics, 2024
claims.where: review text, read via Europe PMC

claims.claim: The vast majority of the body's bacteria live in the colon, and the body holds about 38 trillion bacteria in all.
claims.source: R. Sender, S. Fuchs and R. Milo, "Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body," PLOS Biology, 2016

claims.claim: A 2009 review found no methodologically rigorous controlled trials of colonic cleansing for general health, and said the practice cannot be recommended.

ddw26-rnc-004-hornet-trap.title: Threat, trap, network: the Hornet Trap

summary: Standard baited traps for the yellow-legged hornet catch mostly other insects. In one Italian study the target hornet was 1.02 percent of the catch.
At Dutch Design Week 2026, Accenture showed a prototype trap whose camera would release bees, kill spring queens and tag summer workers.
Tagging workers to find nests has worked in field studies, but no field results for the trap itself were shown.
start_here.how_sure_note: The problem with ordinary traps and the use of tags to find nests come from field studies. The trap itself was a prototype in a demo, with no field results, and this piece makes no claim about how well it works.

claims.claim: Mature nests can produce up to 13,000 individuals over a season, and each can produce up to several hundred potential founder queens.
claims.source: Rome Q and others, "Caste differentiation and seasonal changes in Vespa velutina colonies in its introduced range," Journal of Applied Entomology, 2015
claims.study: 77 nests collected over three years; abstract read

claims.claim: Standard traps caught 213 yellow-legged hornets, 1.02 percent of all insects trapped; bees and their relatives made up 0.13 percent.
claims.source: Lioy S and others, "Effectiveness and Selectiveness of Traps and Baits for Catching the Invasive Hornet Vespa velutina," Insects, 2020
claims.study: field test of two trap types and baits in Liguria, Italy, 2018

claims.claim: The hornet acts as a generalist predator: honeybees 38.1 percent, flies 29.9 percent and social wasps 19.7 percent of prey, with 159 species identified.
claims.source: Rome Q and others, "Not just honeybees: predatory habits of Vespa velutina in France," Annales de la Société entomologique de France, 2021
claims.study: 2,151 prey pellets from 16 nests in south-west France, 2008 to 2010; abstract read

claims.claim: A single hornet nest can consume on average 11.32 kg of insect biomass in one season.
claims.source: Rome Q and others, "Not just honeybees: predatory habits of Vespa velutina in France," Annales de la Société entomologique de France, 2021
claims.study: estimate from prey pellets; abstract read

claims.claim: A harmonic radar following 657 tagged hornets located 11 nests in six of nine localities in Liguria.

claims.claim: VespAI, a camera monitor over a bait station, told yellow-legged hornets from other insects with an F1 score of at least 0.99.

could_be_wrong.point: The trap shown in Eindhoven was a prototype and a proposal. No field results appear in RN's footage of the tour, and none were found in published sources, so this piece makes no claim about how well it works.
The kill, release or tag rule was the demo's. Arvespa writes that Accenture's tracking concepts for Dutch Design Week are a different direction from its own roadmap.
Telling a queen from a worker may be the hardest step. In the Basque study, the two split by size only in late autumn, and size was the only outer difference.
could_be_wrong.source: Pérez-de-Heredia I and others, Journal of Hymenoptera Research 60, 2017

could_be_wrong.point: The 1.02 percent comes from one field study in Liguria in 2018. A 2023 Spanish study found one trap model more selective than the others, though it still judged bait trapping not sustainable.
The diet figures, the 13,000 hornets per nest and the cost figures rest on abstracts only; the full texts were paywalled or behind a bot check.
could_be_wrong.source: Rome Q and others, Annales de la Société entomologique de France, 2021

could_be_wrong.point: Papers give different dates for the hornet's arrival in France: before 2004, 2003, and confirmed since 2005. The mid-2000s is the safe summary.
could_be_wrong.source: Barbet-Massin M, Salles J-M, Courchamp F, NeoBiota, 2020

could_be_wrong.point: Not every expert weighs the threat the same way. A Dutch insect expert wrote in 2025 that the worries had so far proved greatly overstated, in a magazine article rather than a peer-reviewed paper.
VespAI is a different device from the one shown in Eindhoven. It tested the first step, recognizing the hornet, not the full rule.
could_be_wrong.source: O'Shea-Wheller TA and others, Communications Biology 7, 2024

summary: Atelier Fig. invited RN Collins to a breakfast inside Fringe, its Dutch Design Week show.
Fringe grew out of cutting clay with a wire, and the tartlets came on a tray cut into a grid.
The piece follows that grid to the history of anatomical slicing and the lattice of struts inside bone. The link between them is this piece's own.
start_here.how_sure_note: The studio's story comes from its own pages and the festival, and the anatomy from a textbook and published histories. The link between Fringe and bone is this piece's comparison, and the studio never made it.

ddw26-rnc-007-grown-not-made.title: Grown, not made: the Biodesign Warehouse

summary: The Biodesign Warehouse at Dutch Design Week was set up as a department store of things grown by fungi, bacteria and yeast.
Four tables showed a fermenter, a fungal coating still in development, a dye from engineered yeast and a jacket in Ephea, a mycelium material.
Only one of them was already in luxury fashion, and the piece shows how to tell a result from an aim.
start_here.how_sure_note: What each table showed comes from RN's footage and the festival and company pages. Many claims are the makers' own, and no published data could be found for the Fungkee coating or for how Novya's color behaves on skin.

ddw26-rnc-009-stool-society.title: 100 stools and your two sitting bones

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Belgian collective LABO showed about 100 stools by more than 70 makers in Building TX, Eindhoven.
The oldest stool dated from 1970, by the architect Juliaan Lampens, and people have made stools for about 4,000 years.
Every stool rests on the same two bones, the ischial tuberosities, which sit roughly 12 to 14 centimeters apart.
start_here.how_sure_note: The anatomy comes from an open textbook and the show facts from the organizers' own pages. The studies of sitting on stools are small, and one was read as an abstract only.

claims.claim: The outer width between the ischial tuberosities averaged 11.96 cm in men and 13.53 cm in women by an impression method, and 13.42 and 13.30 cm by a seated pressure method.

glossary.plain: The large, rough area at the bottom of the ischium that carries the weight of the body when sitting.
The lower back part of each hip bone, which supports the body when sitting.
The bone on each side of the pelvis, made of three bones, the ilium, the ischium and the pubis, that fuse in the late teenage years.
The three long muscles on the back of the thigh, which start at the ischial tuberosity and flex the knee.
The inward curve of the lower back, which every sitting position in a 2015 X-ray study made smaller.
A curve of the spine that develops after birth, as the lumbar curve does when a child begins to stand and walk.
A style of building that shows raw concrete and leaves out any further decoration, as the heritage commission described the 1970 library in Eke.

ddw26-rnc-011-hamza-guitar-frets.title: Frets for the notes between the notes

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Caro Repr showed RN Collins the HAMZA, a red guitar and the first one they ever built.
A fret sets where a pressed string's vibrating length ends. A standard neck splits the octave into 12 equal steps.
The HAMZA puts frets in other places, for in-between notes used in Middle Eastern and Iranian music, which a player's hand must learn to find.
start_here.how_sure_note: The physics of frets and the hand anatomy come from university and textbook sources. Most facts about the build come from Caro's own account, and the fret positions were not published or measured.

claims.claim: The festival listed the HAMZA as a microtonal baritone guitar with a 27-inch scale, built with Overload Guitars in Rome.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "The HAMZA Guitar," programme page, DDW26

claims.claim: Pressing a string down shortens its effective length and so raises the pitch.
claims.source: Wolfe J, "Strings, standing waves and harmonics," Music Acoustics, University of New South Wales

claims.claim: A standard fretboard approximates equal temperament, with the octave split into 12 equal semitones, each about 1.059 times the last in frequency.
claims.source: Wolfe J, "Acoustics FAQ," Music Acoustics, University of New South Wales

claims.claim: Because real strings deform and are not ideal, perfect intonation of all the notes on a fretted instrument can never be achieved.
claims.source: Varieschi GU, Gower CM, "Intonation and compensation of fretted string instruments," American Journal of Physics 78, no. 1 (2010): 47 to 55
claims.study: tests of fret-placement models on monochord sonometers

claims.claim: Intervals smaller than a semitone are a fundamental difference in Arab music, and the quarter tone may be a regional choice in Egypt.
claims.source: Bozkurt B and colleagues, "An Open Research Dataset of the 1932 Cairo Congress of Arab Music," arXiv 2506.14503 (2025)
claims.study: analysis of the 1932 Cairo Congress audio

claims.claim: In one master singer's shur, steps of 137 and 148 cents sat around a note written with the koron.
claims.source: Shafiei S, "An analysis of Iranian Music Intervals based on Pitch Histogram," arXiv 2108.01283 (2021)
claims.study: pitch histograms of Iranian classical singing

claims.claim: Tar and setar players use 15 to 24 frets per octave, mostly 17 or 18, and Iran has no nationally recognized fretting system.
claims.source: Poorhaydari K, "Empirical Evaluation of Intervals and Fretting Systems in Persian Art Music," Analytical Approaches to World Musics 11, no. 2 (2023)
claims.study: survey of tar players; 19 measured re koron

claims.claim: Tolgahan Çoğulu's 2008 guitar has channels under each string and 150 small frets that can be put in or taken out.
claims.source: Eren O, Güven UZ, "Microtonal Guitar Culture in Turkey," Musicologist 6, no. 1 (2022): 1 to 25
claims.study: interviews with Çoğulu and eight players

claims.claim: The intrinsic muscles of the hand let the fingers make precise movements.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 11.5, "Muscles of the Pectoral Girdle and Upper Limbs"

claims.claim: The lumbricals looked built for high excursion, and the interossei for high force and low excursion.
claims.source: Jacobson MD, Raab R, Fazeli BM, Abrams RA, Botte MJ, Lieber RL, "Architectural design of the human intrinsic hand muscles," Journal of Hand Surgery (American) 17, no. 5 (1992): 804 to 809
claims.study: architecture of 20 muscles, 180 muscles in all; abstract read

summary: Beacons of Hope by Rive Roshan was a set of glass-marquetry columns with moving light, shown in the Klokgebouw at Dutch Design Week 2026.
One of the makers said the team set the pace of the light by feel, and that a version based on data was in the works.
A light that rises and falls like a breath points at the diaphragm and the rib muscles that make each breath.

summary: Shown at Dutch Design Week 2026, Everything Moist Seems Alive by MAISON the FAUX and Studio Boris Acket filled a dark hall at MU with mist, pools and a choir.
The work drew on Astrida Neimanis's idea of hydrofeminism, which treats bodies as open, leaky bodies of water.
An anatomy textbook gives adults about 50 to 60 percent water, and shows how a body takes water in and sends it out every day.
start_here.how_sure_note: The sixty percent the festival gave is the makers' own figure, at the top of the textbook's adult range, so that number is less sure than the rest. The other body facts come from an open anatomy textbook, and the room's details from the makers, MU, the festival, Dezeen and RN Collins's own footage.
start_here.how_sure_approved: RN approved Nov 24: how sure set from "strong" to "moderate"; note rewritten in plain words to give the reason

claims.claim: Human beings are mostly water, from about 75 percent of body mass in infants to about 50 to 60 percent in adults, and as low as 45 percent in old age.

claims.claim: The fluid inside cells makes up about 60 percent of the body's water, about 25 liters in an average-size adult male.
claims.source: J. Gordon Betts and others, Anatomy and Physiology, OpenStax, 2013, section 26.1, "Body Fluids and Fluid Compartments"

claims.claim: The brain and kidneys are 80 to 85 percent water, and teeth are 8 to 10 percent.
claims.source: J. Gordon Betts and others, Anatomy and Physiology, OpenStax, 2013, section 26.1, "Body Fluids and Fluid Compartments"

claims.claim: An average adult takes in about 2,500 mL of water a day, makes about 230 mL inside the body, and loses about 2,500 mL, most of it as urine.
claims.source: J. Gordon Betts and others, Anatomy and Physiology, OpenStax, 2013, section 26.2, "Water Balance"

claims.claim: Connection between watery bodies happens as water crosses only partially permeable membranes.

summary: During Dutch Design Week 2026, the ceramic collective Off World showed Wonderland ceramics by Minjeong Park and Radina Putri at Galerie Nasty Alice in Eindhoven.
The work titles follow Carroll's two Alice books, and his text calls the hat maker only "the Hatter," a man who kept hats to sell.
The piece also follows mercury in real felt hat making and the line between ceramics and porcelain on the work list.
start_here.how_sure_note: The show, the works and the Carroll quotations rest on the festival and gallery pages, the printed work list and the books themselves. The link between the Hatter and mercury poisoning is disputed: a U.S. agency makes it, and a 1989 historian doubts it.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the TU Delft student team Emergence Delft showed two works: Illumina, about the glass fiber under the internet, and SYNC, about the pumps that keep low Dutch land dry.
RN Collins did not see the works. The piece is built from the program, the press kit, the team's own pages and the public sources behind both systems.
It explains how glass holds light, where undersea cables reach the Dutch coast, why drained land keeps sinking and how screws, wind and steam drained the polders.
start_here.how_sure_note: The physics, the history and the government figures come from primary sources that were read in full. What the two works did comes only from the team's own pages and the press kit, because the works were not seen in person. Two of the team's figures stay theirs, and one water board figure is given as a trade magazine reported it.

glossary.plain: A thread of very pure glass that carries light. A typical fiber is about 125 micrometers across, with a core of about 10 micrometers.
When light inside a material meets the edge at more than the critical angle, it does not leave. It reflects back inside, which is how a fiber keeps its light.
A layer of glass with a lower index of refraction around a fiber's core. It keeps the light inside even when fibers in a bundle press together.
A cable on or under the seabed, with glass fibers inside layers of plastic and sometimes steel wire. In the open ocean it is about as wide as a garden hose.
Low land kept dry by drainage. A polder below sea level needs its rain and seepage pumped up into a canal and out to sea.
The one reference level that all Dutch heights are measured against. A height of 0 meters NAP is about the average level of the North Sea.
A shaft with helical blades turning in a sloping trough. In a windmill, an open screw could lift water four to five meters.
The sinking of drained peat soil. In rural areas, lowering the groundwater is its main cause, and it also releases carbon dioxide.

ddw26-rnc-1001-robot-writes-gas-history.title: A robot that writes and wipes history

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Groningen studio Paul&Albert showed Writing History, a robot arm that wrote on glass with a marker and wiped it with a sponge.
The festival page said it wrote Groningen gas headlines, but the studio and the host show described other texts, and no source said which ran that week.
The piece sets the press kit's gas story beside the parliamentary inquiry, its historians, two newspaper studies and the 2024 law that ended production.
start_here.how_sure_note: The gas history rests on official papers read page by page: the inquiry, the historians' analysis, the 1993 report and the laws. What the robot wrote is less sure, because its three public descriptions do not match and no list of its texts was published.

claims.claim: The festival page called Writing History an autonomous robotic installation by Paul&Albert for Museum aan de A, writing newspaper headlines about gas extraction in Groningen from 1959 to the present.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Writing History," programme page, DDW26

claims.claim: The studio said the arm drew on a database of historical facts and illustrations from Groningen and responded to live water level, traffic and weather data; its page did not mention gas.
claims.source: Paul&Albert, "Writing History"

claims.claim: Manifestations called the Eindhoven version a special MUTE edition made with Museum aan de A, writing texts about censorship, silence, power and suppressed voices.
claims.source: Manifestations, 2026 programme

claims.claim: The arm wrote with a marker and wiped with a sponge inside a vitrine made of 200 kilos of steel, with a magnetic spring system balancing marker, gripper and glass.
claims.source: Paul&Albert, "Writing History"

claims.claim: Gas was found near Slochteren on 22 July 1959, and NAM began producing gas from the field in 1963.

claims.claim: A member of parliament, A.W. Biewenga, asked about the risk of subsidence in October 1962, and NAM's confidential research then sat in a drawer for years.

claims.claim: On 7 May 1987 minister Smit-Kroes answered that the Slochteren field was too far away to have caused the shock felt in Assen.
claims.source: Aanhangsel Handelingen II 1986/87, nr. 669

claims.claim: An official research committee concluded in November 1993 that under certain conditions earthquakes are the result of gas production.
claims.source: Begeleidingscommissie Onderzoek Aardbevingen, Eindrapport, 1993

claims.claim: A study of 2,265 articles from five Dutch newspapers, 1990 to 2015, found that about one article in ten set money against safety before 2013 and almost one in three by 2015.
claims.source: Opperhuizen, Schouten and Klijn, Journalism Studies, 2018
claims.study: peer-reviewed content analysis, hand-coded sample plus a trained computer model

claims.claim: The tipping point in media reporting did not follow an increase in the risk; the likely trigger was the mining regulator's report of January 2013.
claims.source: Opperhuizen and Schouten, Quality & Quantity, 2020

claims.claim: The parliamentary inquiry, which reported on 24 February 2023, found that the interests of the people of Groningen had been structurally ignored.
claims.source: Tweede Kamer, Groningers boven gas, part 1

glossary.plain: A robot installation by the studio Paul&Albert, made for Museum aan de A. An industrial robot arm in a glass case wrote with a marker and wiped the words away with a sponge.
A Dutch design duo from Groningen, Paul Mulder and Albert Buring. They make exhibitions, installations and objects for museums, companies, governments and collectors.

The museum that took over from the northern shipping museum in Groningen in 2020. It plans a new museum about the history of the city and province of Groningen, and its building was closed for a rebuild.
Manifestations was the art and technology show on floor 8 of the VEEM building at Dutch Design Week. Its 2026 theme, MUTE, asked how technology shapes what people hear, say and share.
The company that produced the gas from the Groningen field, starting in 1963.
Dutch for the gas building: the name later given to the partnership between the state and the oil companies that are now Shell and ExxonMobil.
A study of the language and framing in the news and in politics. Historians at Radboud University wrote one on Groningen gas from 1959 to 2022 for the parliamentary inquiry.
The national mining regulator. In January 2013 it advised that gas production should go down as fast as was realistic to protect people in Groningen.

law_policy.status: Article 52c of the Mining Act: no more gas is produced from the Groningen field. Also sets aftercare duties and changes the Civil Code time limit for damage claims.
The ban took effect on 19 April 2024; the measuring and aftercare parts were left for later.
The measuring and aftercare parts took effect on 1 October 2025.

ddw26-rnc-1002-one-shared-wage.title: One shared wage, one big body

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, The Collective Response at Foundation We Are in Eindhoven put four works side by side on how people act together.
The piece follows the Rotterdam studio Extra Practice's shared income pool, a body printed in ship dazzle, and a table on citizens' assemblies, back to the public documents behind each.
It is built from the makers' own pages, the festival's pages and press kits, and public documents; RN Collins has no footage of the show.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every fact was checked against its source text, most of them word for word. But The Pool is known only from the festival's and the studio's own words, and neither published the size of the wage, the share of income that goes in or how the money is held. The dazzle history rests on the Navy's own documents, whose editors doubt it ever worked.

claims.claim: The Collective Response ran at Foundation We Are, Torenallee 22-04, Strijp-S, Eindhoven, with four works by Yamuna Forzani, Questions Collective (Tessel Brühl), Extra Practice and Bureau Burgerberaad.

claims.claim: The festival said Extra Practice started "The Pool": they pour all their income into one bank account and redistribute it as a stable monthly wage.

claims.source: Broodfonds, "Hoe het werkt"

claims.claim: In 2021 to 2023, an average of 194,000 people a year worked as artists in the Netherlands; 56 percent were self-employed without staff, and 27 percent had a gross yearly income under 20,000 euros, against 19 percent of all workers.

claims.claim: The national climate assembly met first on 18 January 2025 with 175 people, worked over seven weekends and handed in its advice on 1 December 2025; the cabinet said it would adopt half of the proposals.
claims.source: Kamerbrief, 29 May 2026

claims.claim: The assembly made 23 recommendations; 13 were adopted with more than 75 percent support, and they break down into 82 sub-recommendations.

claims.claim: An independent evaluation found about 25 percent of people surveyed had heard of the assembly, only 8 percent knew the cabinet had responded, and it takes three to five years to tell how much such advice becomes policy.

A Dutch group of 20 to 50 self-employed people who know each other. Each sets aside a fixed sum every month, and a member who is sick for a long time gets gifts from the others for up to two years.
The Dutch cultural sector's code on fair work, launched in 2017. It rests on five values and three principles: fair pay, fair share and fair chain.
Bold, broken paint on ships in both world wars. It did not try to hide a ship. It tried to make an attacker misjudge the ship's size and course.

The rule of lights and shadows named for Abbott Thayer, whose 1902 patent with Gerome Brush painted a ship's lit surfaces dark and shaded ones light. Wilkinson's letter says dazzle still used it in places.
A group of residents chosen by lot who together form a cross-section of society. They meet over some months, talk with experts and each other, and make recommendations.
The second step of choosing an assembly. Among the residents who answer an invitation, the draw takes account of traits such as age, region and background.
A person who works for themselves and employs no one. In 2021 to 2023, 56 percent of Dutch artists worked this way.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Design Museum Gent brought the story of its new gate, Freeze Frame 82.2 by the Antwerp studio Unfold: an aluminum curtain frozen just before opening.
The piece follows the gate back through the printing method behind it, a robot arm laying metal with a welding arc, and what tests of that method have shown.
It ends at the 1755 town house behind the gate and the new wing's rooms, down to the toilets, which the press kit says about twenty designers shaped.
start_here.how_sure_note: The facts about the gate itself, including the 250 kilogram weight, are the museum's own and no one else has published a check of them. The printing method and the house's history rest on peer-reviewed papers and official heritage files. RN Collins has no footage of the stand, so nothing here comes from her own tape.

glossary.plain: Unfold's aluminum gate for the new wing of Design Museum Gent. Its name is the frame where a digital curtain simulation was stopped, just before opening.
3D printing with welding tools. An electric arc melts the tip of a metal wire, and a robot moves the torch so each pass leaves a bead of metal on the last.
How much metal a printer lays down in an hour. For the MX3D steel bridge it was generally 0.5 to 2.0 kilograms an hour.
The rippled surface a printed metal part has before it is machined. In tests on the bridge's steel, as-built strips were generally weaker and less stiff, by up to about 20 percent.
Small gas bubbles trapped in metal as it cools. A 2021 study said they make printing aluminum with an arc quite challenging.
The museum's name for the works it commissioned for its new building, such as the reception desk, the pocket garden and the toilets.
The museum's main building, an 18th-century town house on Jan Breydelstraat in Ghent. The city bought it in 1920, and the museum moved in three years later.
A lime-cured brick made from local municipal waste that hardens without a kiln. It forms the facade of the new wing.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Brohwyn Brennan's Tools for Collapse showed two kits for a story set in 2081 on the Falsterbo peninsula in Sweden: ESCAPE, a mock luxury kit, and STAY, a raft for shared repair.
RN Collins has no footage of the work. Everything about the kits comes from the festival's programme page and press kit.
The piece then checks the story against the real wall Vellinge began building in 2024, the 1872 storm flood, SMHI's sea level figures and studies of who leaves in a flood.
start_here.how_sure_note: What the kits are and what they mean comes only from the designer's own project text, so that part is less sure. The facts about the real wall, the 1872 flood and sea levels rest on the municipality's own pages, SVT and TV4 reports, SMHI reports and published papers, each checked against the source text. Official sources give different lengths and end dates for the wall, so the piece gives each figure.
start_here.how_sure_approved: RN approved Nov 24: how sure set from "strong" to "moderate"; note rewritten in plain words to give the reason

glossary.plain: Building objects for a future that has not happened, so that people can argue about it now. The project text called its method a comparative speculative design framework.
A future technology that exists only inside a film's story world but works there as a real object. The term comes from a 2010 paper by David A. Kirby.
The press kit's name for the comfortable idea that climate breakdown can be solved or designed away.
Sealing the seams where a wooden boat's planks meet. Fiber made from teased-out hemp was hammered into the seams and sealed with hot pitch. Synthetic resins are now often used in place of pitch.
Swedish for the protective embankment. It is the name of the real wall Vellinge began building on the Falsterbo peninsula in 2024, and the name the story gives its wall.

A Representative Concentration Pathway, one of two middle paths used in climate science. The number is the extra heating effect from human activity, in watts per square meter, at the end of the century. It is not a forecast.
A Shared Socioeconomic Pathway in which large inequalities within and across countries dominate. The paired scenario SSP4-6.0 updates the RCP6.0 pathway.
The storm surge of November 1872, perhaps the best known in Swedish waters. It killed around 300 people along the coasts of Skåne, Denmark and Germany.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Irish design office Studio Saol showed The Pluriversity, a model of the Shannon region imagined as the campuses of a university in 2070.
The project began as a strategy job for a major Irish university and grew through three years of research, a futures report with eight scenarios and a set of workshop tools.
RN Collins has no footage of the work, so the piece follows it through the festival page, the press kit, the project's website and the reports behind it.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every line was checked against the festival page, the press kit and the project's own reports, but most of what is known comes from the makers themselves. No independent review was found, the English and Dutch materials lists disagree, and RN Collins has no footage of the model.

glossary.plain: Studio Saol's imagined university for the Shannon region in 2070: a plural, networked, place-rooted institution, meant to co-exist with the university and not replace it.
A place defined by its land and water, and the ideas about how to live there. Berg and Dasmann proposed a river's watershed as the frame for a community.
The Pluriversity's unit of learning: an applied space where new ways of running a place could be tried in the real world, each lab taking on one system, such as food or energy.
The project's set of workshop tools, drawn from the World Café, that took its ideas to students, staff and local people.
A model, credited to the Dutch researcher Frank Geels, in which big outside pressures push on an old system and small experiments at the edges can then grow.
Oak from Irish peat bogs, called black oak because iron in the groundwater stains it. The trees grew on living bogs, blew down and were buried in the peat.
Aaron Antonovsky's idea, as the position paper put it: the study of the factors that generate well-being, beyond the prevention of disease.
The study of how all the structures in one body region, such as the abdomen, relate to one another.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the artist Yvonne Mak stacked hundreds of sandbags into a castle on the lake at the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, and every bag was cast in concrete.
The piece reads flood manuals on what a sandbag can and cannot do, a UN Environment Programme report on why cement costs carbon, and a review of concrete that seals its own cracks.
RN Collins has no footage of this work, so what is said about the castle comes from the festival's pages, its press kit and the partners' own statements.
start_here.how_sure_note: The science on cement and on crack sealing comes from a UN report and a large review, checked page by page. What is in the castle rests on the festival's own texts, which give two different counts, and no one has said which bag uses which product. Company claims are given as the companies' own words.

glossary.plain: Yvonne Mak's work at Dutch Design Week 2026: a castle of sandbag shapes, every one cast in concrete, on a raft on the Van Abbemuseum lake in Eindhoven.
The main part of ordinary Portland cement, made by heating ground clay and limestone to a high temperature. The heat drives CO2 out of the limestone itself.
A powder, such as fine limestone, blast-furnace slag or fly ash, that replaces part of the clinker in cement.
Clay heated to about 700 to 850 °C so that it becomes reactive. Mixed with ground limestone, it can replace up to half the clinker, the report's authors said.
A binder that skips clinker and is activated with alkalis. The UNEP report said its commercial use was still very small and most real mixes relied on slag.
A large concrete box. Caissons closed the biggest dike gaps after the 1953 flood in the Netherlands.
A powder added to fresh concrete that reacts with water and cement to grow crystals in pores and fine cracks. A 2018 review called it a trade label whose ingredients are usually not disclosed.
Bacterial spores and calcium salts mixed into concrete. When water enters a crack, the bacteria turn the salt into calcium carbonate, which is limestone.
The bridge of cartilage and bone that forms between the broken ends of a bone and is later replaced by bone.
A rule that says what a concrete must do, such as its strength and durability, and leaves the recipe open.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Melyssa Lim showed Vis à vis, a two-seat chair bent from metal tube into a snake with a brass head at each end.
RN Collins has no footage of it, so the piece reads the chair from the festival's page, the maker's own text, a 2020 interview and two press photos.
It then follows the chair's shape back through seats for two since the 1780s, the metalwork the festival names and the body of the snake.
start_here.how_sure_note: The history, the metalwork words and the snake biology rest on museum collection data, the Getty vocabulary and papers, each checked line by line. What is said about the chair itself rests only on the festival's page, the maker's own words and two press photos, which give no size, materials or method for each part.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Studio RENS showed STILLS, wall works made with Tarkett linoleum that put the backing, fibers, cut edges and colors in view.
RN Collins has no footage of the show, so STILLS is read from the festival's program page, the press kit and the studio's own page.
The rest follows the material: its recipe, its factories, the tests buyers ran on its back and edges, and its earlier lives on walls.
start_here.how_sure_note: The history rests on period documents read in full, such as a 1928 factory booklet, a 1924 federal specification and the 1878 judgment. What STILLS looked like rests only on the festival's and makers' own pages and two press photos, which give no sizes, prices or count of works.

glossary.plain: Wall works by Studio RENS made with Tarkett linoleum, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026. The festival text said they brought forward the backing, fibers, edges, cuts and colors normally kept out of sight.
The 2023 research in which Studio RENS and Tarkett explored the hidden side of linoleum. STILLS continued where it left off.
A floor made mainly of linseed oil, cork and jute. Its inventor, Frederick Walton, built the name from two Latin words, "linum," flax, and "oleum," oil.
The reaction in which oils react with oxygen from the air. In drying oils such as linseed oil, the chains link to one another until they form a network, and a film forms.
Oxidized linseed oil mixed with resin. Tarkett says it oxidizes pine resin and linseed oil together for 24 hours, then mixes the cement with cork and wood flour, limestone flour and pigments.
The woven jute backing of linoleum. The 1928 Sloane booklet called the burlap back "one identification of genuine linoleum."
Pressing the warm mix of cement, cork flour and pigment onto a strip of burlap between two huge rollers.
Hanging fresh sheets in heated rooms until they hardened. The Sloane plant took two to eight weeks; Tarkett says its sheets dry for at least 20 days.
Linoleum whose colors "go clear through to the back." Printed linoleum carried its pattern only on the surface.
A thinner wall covering that Walton patented in 1877, made from oxidized linseed oil and embossed by rollers so that, once painted, it could pass for tooled leather, carved wood, metal or plaster.

law_policy.citation: Linoleum Manufacturing Company v. Nairn (1878) 7 Ch. D. 834 (Fry, J., 30 January 1878)
law_policy.status: Action dismissed. The court held that the word names the substance, so a rival free to make it could sell it by that name.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Carla Schwering showed The Voice from the Water, woven hangings built on Anna Gmeyner's 1932 play Automatenbüfett.
RN Collins has no footage of this work, so the piece reads the program page, the press kit and other public sources.
It follows three threads back to where they start: a writer the stage lost, a blue print made by sunlight, and a loom that read punched cards.
start_here.how_sure_note: The history parts were checked line by line against old papers, museum catalogs and Gmeyner's own 1939 account. The play's plot comes from three theater and press pages that agree. No copy of the 1932 text was open to read. What the woven pieces mean comes from the maker's own press kit, and RN Collins has no footage of the work.

glossary.plain: A photographic print that turns blue where light reaches paper treated with iron salts. Sir John Herschel named it in 1842.
A picture made by laying an object on treated paper in strong light, without a camera. Anna Atkins made up to ten thousand of them with seaweed.
A loom whose pattern is set by a computer. The maker of one model, the TC2, said its software maps every pixel of an image to individual threads.
In a Jacquard loom, a card whose holes let pins pass through to lift some warp threads and not others, one card for each pass of the weft.
A snack bar that sold food and drink from machines but still needed human labor. It was also the title of Anna Gmeyner's 1932 play.
The Latin root the press kit gave for both "text" and "textile". Lewis and Short give the verb texo first as "to weave".
In 1932 the Kleist Prize was split between Richard Billinger and Else Lasker-Schüler. Gmeyner received an honorable mention for Automatenbüfett, not the prize.

summary: Hotel Mariënhage in Eindhoven sits in the former school and chapel buildings of an Augustinian monastery complex with a 15th-century wing.
The site may have held a castle mound from about 1100, became a monastery around 1420, burned in 1581 and was restored as a hotel and ceremony house.
A robot dog in a corridor painting leads to a dog's real anatomy: the joint that looks like a backward knee is the ankle, the hock.
start_here.how_sure_note: The building history rests on the national monument register, a province statement and two archaeology reports, and the dog anatomy on peer-reviewed papers. Where sources differ, such as 1419 or 1420, the piece gives both.

ddw26-rnc-1010-lamps-from-old-fabric.title: Lamps sewn from fabric someone threw away

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, KALUMA, a young studio from The Hague, showed VELA, a set of lamps made from discarded fabric.
The piece reads the studio's festival page, press kit and shop pages, then the textile waste figures and the Dutch and EU rules around old cloth.
It also traces the two older ideas the lamps borrow from: the Gifu paper lantern behind Noguchi's Akari, and the Space Age saucer of the Evoluon in Eindhoven.
start_here.how_sure_note: The law, waste figures and history come from primary texts read in full. What the piece says about the lamps rests on KALUMA's own kit and pages: RN Collins has no footage of them, and no outside review or test was found.

claims.claim: KALUMA showed VELA, lamps made from discarded fabric, at Sectie-C in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week 2026.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "VELA | Lighting from Reclaimed Textiles," participant page, DDW26

claims.claim: KALUMA collaborated with local ateliers and thrift stores to source discarded fabrics sourced locally in the Netherlands.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2360, VELA, hosted by KALUMA

claims.claim: Each textile was assessed for quality, color and suitability, then taken apart and reworked by hand in the studio in The Hague, and differently sized objects let even smaller textile waste be used.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2360, VELA, hosted by KALUMA

claims.claim: The VELA pendant combined reclaimed fabric with a 3D-printed structure of plant-based PLA, and the table lamp added aluminum legs and a socket cover.
claims.source: KALUMA, VELA Pendant; KALUMA, VELA Table Lamp

claims.claim: Of the textile waste the EU produced in 2020, 82 percent had been used as clothing or household textiles.
claims.source: European Environment Agency, "Management of used and waste textiles in Europe's circular economy," 2024

claims.claim: Leftovers and textile waste from garment production ranged from 25 to 40 percent of the fabric used, depending on factory size, and about half could be upcycled in the authors' experiments.
claims.source: Aus et al., Fashion and Textiles 2021

claims.claim: The Dutch textile decree took effect on 1 July 2023 and requires at least 50 percent of the clothing and household linen a producer put on the market the year before to be prepared for reuse or recycled in 2025, rising to 75 percent from 2030.
claims.source: Besluit uitgebreide producentenverantwoordelijkheid textiel, BWBR0048093

claims.claim: Directive (EU) 2025/1892 makes producer responsibility for textiles compulsory across the EU, to be brought into national law by 17 June 2027; its product list does not include lamps.
claims.source: Directive (EU) 2025/1892

claims.claim: Isamu Noguchi arrived in Gifu in 1951, put an electric bulb where the lantern's candle had been, and called the series Akari.
claims.source: Noguchi Museum, "The History of Akari Light Sculptures"

claims.claim: The Evoluon, designed by Louis Kalff and Leo de Bever for Philips, opened on 24 September 1966, and Kalff said he "thought about future, weightlessness, science fiction."
claims.source: Philips Museum, "The Evoluon. A good idea has many fathers"

claims.claim: PLA textiles did not degrade in seawater for more than 428 days in tests at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography pier.
claims.source: Royer et al., PLOS ONE 2023

could_be_wrong.point: Everything about how VELA was made comes from KALUMA's own kit and pages. RN Collins has no footage of the lamps, and no independent review, press coverage or test of their light or safety was found.
could_be_wrong.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2360, VELA, hosted by KALUMA

could_be_wrong.point: The kit says the cloth came from ateliers and thrift stores, while the pendant page says local production waste and offcuts. Whether thrift-store cloth is in the lamps sold online is not stated, and no amounts, fibers or cleaning steps are published.
The shop page calls the PLA frame biodegradable. The seawater study shows that depends on conditions, but it tested seawater only, so it says nothing direct about soil or a home compost heap.
The waste shares are EU-wide and factory-level figures. None of them measures the cloth in VELA, and the EEA says Member States report very little data on pre-consumer waste.
The Dutch circular textile mission rests on the abstract of Reike et al. and the university's summary; the full paper could not be opened.
The tie between VELA and the Evoluon is the piece's own reading. KALUMA does not mention the Evoluon, and nothing in its texts links the lamps to it.

glossary.plain: KALUMA's collection of pendant and table lamps made from discarded fabric on 3D-printed frames, shown at Dutch Design Week 2026.
A workroom, such as a tailor's or a seamstress's studio. KALUMA named local ateliers as one source of its cloth.
Cloth that leaves the chain before anyone uses it, such as cutting waste, roll ends or unsold fabric.
Cloth that was used as clothing or household textiles and then thrown out. It made up 82 percent of the EU's textile waste in 2020.
A rule that makes the firms that sell a product pay for and arrange what happens to it as waste. The Netherlands set one for clothing and household linen from 1 July 2023.
Polylactic acid, a plant-based plastic. VELA's frames were 3D-printed from it.
The Japanese word for a paper lantern. In Gifu they were made by hand with thin washi paper on bamboo frames.
Isamu Noguchi's series of paper lamps, begun in Gifu in 1951. The word means light and also suggests weightlessness.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Studio Jeroen Wand opened its Eindhoven building and showed Re-Veneer, furniture pressed from leftover veneer all the way through.
The piece follows the material: what veneer is for, how a log is cut into it, why thin layers behave as they do and where the scraps go.
RN Collins has no footage of this work, so the post is built from the festival's pages, the studio's press kit and published sources.
start_here.how_sure_note: The facts about veneer, plywood and mill waste come from an industry manual, a government handbook and a peer-reviewed paper, and the museum details from the museums' own pages, all checked line by line. What is known about Re-Veneer itself rests on the studio's short press text and a few interviews: no source gives its glue, layer order, where the offcuts come from or how the pieces wear.

claims.claim: The studio's press text said pieces of leftover veneer are pressed together in a specific mold, combined with solid wooden parts, so that veneer is used throughout the whole object.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2052, Collections, Studio Jeroen Wand

claims.claim: Collections ran at Studio Jeroen Wand, Bayeuxlaan 7, Eindhoven, from 17 to 25 October 2026, 11:00 to 18:00 each day, with free access.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Collections," programme page, DDW26

claims.claim: Most solid boards for tabletops are 25 mm thick and veneer is usually about 0.6 mm thick, so about 40 slices of veneer can come from the wood of one board.
claims.source: FWPA, A Manual for Decorative Wood Veneering Technology, 2013

claims.claim: Plywood is built from sheets of veneer with the grain of adjacent layers at right angles, to even out shrinkage and improve its engineering properties.
claims.source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, 2021, ch. 11; FWPA 2013

claims.claim: Wood barely shrinks along the grain (0.1% to 0.2% for most species) but far more across it: 5.5% radial and 7.8% tangential for black walnut.
claims.source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, 2021, ch. 4

claims.claim: Veneer mill waste was used routinely as fuel, only 10% of clippings were recycled into composite products, and 15 mills in the central Appalachian region made about 60,000 metric tons of clipping residue a year.
claims.source: Denes, Lang and McNeel, BioResources 12, no. 1 (2017)
claims.where: introduction; the survey figure is cited from Hassler 2002

claims.claim: Jeroen Wand said the veneer for his products is "a residual stream that would otherwise go into the stove," that the glue has to be as environmentally friendly as possible and that the workshop runs on solar power.
claims.source: Vij5, "Designer interview: Jeroen Wand," 26 June 2023
claims.study: interview published by a furniture label

claims.claim: The studio said Wand made the Paper Chair in 2006 from layers of paper with a laminating technique borrowed from the wood industry, and that this led to the idea of making a solid material from leftover veneer.
claims.source: Studio Jeroen Wand, "aluminium chair," portfolio page

claims.claim: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen holds a Laminated Table by Wand dated 2015, listed as veneer and glue, bought in 2017 with Mondriaan Fund support.
claims.source: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Laminated Table, V 3193

claims.claim: The Cabinet with Inlaid Flower Vases, attributed to Jan van Mekeren, has an oak body veneered with many woods, and its wood gave felling dates between 1693 and 1703.
claims.source: Rijksmuseum, BK-1964-12; Hagelskamp and van Duin, Rijksmuseum Bulletin 2012
claims.study: museum entry and conservators' tree-ring study

claims.claim: Phases of Laura was a rawer version of Wand's Phases vases, with Laura's colors and the mold's natural wear and tear kept in the design, as a tribute to Folkert de Jong's 2007 Balancing Act of Laura.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2052, Collections, Studio Jeroen Wand

could_be_wrong.point: The press kit does not name the venue of the photo of the Re-Veneer column; the file's camera data dates it to 4 March 2026. It should not be read as a picture of the Dutch Design Week show.

could_be_wrong.point: The press text speaks of a specific mold, while MaterialDistrict says the studio uses a vacuum technique that needs no difficult molds. Both can be true, but neither shows the studio's setup.

No source names the glue. Wand said only that it has to be as environmentally friendly as possible. The FWPA manual notes that urea formaldehyde, a common veneering glue, can release formaldehyde gas under certain conditions; whether Re-Veneer uses it is not public.

No source found gives where the offcuts come from, which species they are, how the layers are oriented or how the pieces hold up over years of use. Those matter for any laminated product, because wood moves across the grain.
could_be_wrong.source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, 2021, ch. 4

could_be_wrong.point: The mill survey figure covers 15 mills in one region of the United States and is cited secondhand from Hassler 2002. It does not say where the studio's veneer comes from.
The ARC19 award for the Laminated Coffee Table rests on the studio's own statement; no page from the award's organizer was found.

glossary.plain: A thin slice of wood cut from a log by peeling, slicing or sawing, with its thickness set by what it will be used for.
The plainer panel under a veneer, such as medium density fiberboard, particleboard or plywood. It gives the panel stability and strength.
Pieces of veneer laid over the whole surface of an object to form patterns, designs or pictures.
Turning a log against a knife so the veneer comes off like a ribbon, very wide and with a bold grain.
A flat panel built from sheets of veneer called plies, with the grain of each layer at right angles to the next.
A product in which every veneer layer runs the same way, hot pressed into long lengths.
The strips cut off when bundles of veneer are trimmed to a clean rectangle, on average 1 to 4 m long and 25 to 50 mm wide.
Studio Jeroen Wand's furniture of leftover veneer, pressed in a mold with solid wooden parts so the veneer runs through the whole object.
The studio's technique for its Phases vases: a shape cast from one mold, then dipped in fresh plaster until the outside turned rough.

ddw26-rnc-1012-furniture-for-temporary-r.title: Furniture for rooms you will leave

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Spotnik Collection showed a lamp for compact, temporary rooms, made for students and young professionals.
The maker's own site said it was built from a standard aluminum rail, 3D-printed modules and a reclaimed street-light shade.
Dutch figures and lease rules described the rooms it was made for, and how the rules for temporary student leases changed from 2024.
start_here.how_sure_note: The housing figures and lease rules come from official texts, each read in full. Everything about the lamp comes from the maker's and the festival's own words and photos: RN Collins has no footage of the stand, and nothing tested how the lamp works or comes apart.

claims.claim: Dutch Design Week 2026 listed the Spotnik Collection, hosted by Charlie Starman Product Design, in the Piet Hein Eek building at Halvemaanstraat 30 in Eindhoven.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Spotnik Collection," participant page, DDW26

claims.claim: The press text said the collection was "designed for compact and temporary living spaces, particularly for students and young professionals."
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2429, Spotnik Collection

claims.claim: The project "started from observing everyday domestic habits," and those gestures became functions in the design.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2429, Spotnik Collection

claims.claim: The maker's site called the lamp a "modular floor lamp" built on standard aluminium T-slot extrusion profiles, with two 3D-printed modules: one holding "a discarded street-light diffuser," the other a hook for everyday objects.
claims.source: Charlie Starman Product Design, website

claims.claim: The two Spotnik Dock files in the press kit carry the software tag "KeyShot 14," so they are computer renders and the piece does not show them.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2429, Spotnik Collection

claims.claim: The festival credited the design to Carlo Mazzoleni Theocharis, who studied Industrial Product Design at the Politecnico di Milano from 2021 to 2024.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Spotnik Collection," participant page, DDW26; Charlie Starman Product Design, website

claims.claim: On 3 July 1669, Amsterdam's city council agreed to a proposal by Jan van der Heyden to install 2,556 street lamps.
claims.source: CODART, "Unique Collection of Objects of Jan van der Heyden Acquired by the Amsterdam City Archives and Amsterdam Museum," 7 February 2020

claims.source: Victoria and Albert Museum, "Toio," standard lamp

claims.claim: More than 174,000 young people aged 18 to 30 left their parents' home in 2024; 31.5 percent were students, whose most common first home was a private rental, at 49.9 percent.
claims.source: CBS, "Amsterdam populairste bestemming jongeren die uit huis gaan," 28 September 2026

claims.claim: Almost 5,000 new places for students were built in 2025, and the shortage fell to about 20,200 student homes.
claims.source: Rijksoverheid, "Bijna 5000 nieuwe studentenwoningen in 2025," 3 September 2026
claims.study: government release on the national monitor

claims.claim: From 1 July 2024, a fixed-term lease no longer ends just because its term has run out, except a lease of two years or less for groups named by decree, including students who move to another municipality for their studies.
claims.source: Wet vaste huurcontracten, Staatsblad 2023, 480; Besluit specifieke groepen tijdelijke huurovereenkomst, Staatsblad 2024, 152, with explanatory note

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Eindhoven artist Lynn van der Vleuten showed Steentijd, brick cylinders set on steel wire so they seemed to float.
Her press kit said brick had largely lost its load-bearing job. The piece checks that against Dutch sources on clay, kilns, color and walls.
RN Collins has no footage of the work, so the installation is described from the festival page, the press kit and the artist's own site.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every fact was checked against its source: a geology paper, building histories, the brick makers' technical sheets, the national monument register and a government inspectorate report. The installation itself is known only from the festival page, the press kit and the artist's site, since there is no footage of it.

claims.claim: Steentijd was a brick installation by the Eindhoven artist Lynn van der Vleuten, shown in Hall G at Sectie-C during Dutch Design Week 2026.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Steentijd," participant page, DDW26
claims.study: festival page hosted by the artist

claims.claim: The press kit said the cylinders balanced on steel wire, differed in color and stood at different heights, and that the building block rose above "its former, largely lost, load-bearing function."
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2659, Steentijd

claims.claim: In drying, shaped clay lost 20 to 35% of its mass as water and shrank by 3 to 10% in length, and kilns reached top temperatures of 1,000 to 1,200 degrees Celsius.
claims.source: van Wijck 1993
claims.study: journal article on Dutch brick clay

claims.claim: For the brick industry, the Holocene river sediments of the Maas and the Rhine were by far the most important, and much clay that suits ceramics was laid down in the floodplains after dike building began, from about 1200 AD.
claims.source: van Wijck 1993
claims.study: journal article on Dutch brick clay

claims.claim: As the ratio of iron oxide to calcium oxide drops from 1.0 to 0.3, the fired color shifts from red, through bronze, to yellow.
claims.source: van Wijck 1993
claims.study: journal article on Dutch brick clay

claims.claim: When bricks cool through 573 degrees, quartz shrinks by 2.4% in volume, which can crack a brick that cools unevenly.
claims.source: van Wijck 1993
claims.study: journal article on Dutch brick clay

claims.claim: The ring kiln was invented in 1858 by F.E. Hoffmann.
claims.source: Lex, "ringovn"

claims.claim: The ring kiln at De Werklust near Losser was built in 1928, with a brick chimney of about 45 meters, and the register called it one of the few ring kilns in Europe still working.
claims.source: Rijksmonumentenregister, monument 513489

claims.claim: The textbook case of early Dutch brick, Klaarkamp from 1163, used tuff in its first phase, and the rise of brick in the Low Countries is placed at around 1200.
claims.source: van Tussenbroek 2008

claims.claim: From the start of the 20th century, the main Dutch wall was the full cavity wall of two half-brick skins, in which the inner skin is the bearing wall.
claims.source: Kooij 1996

claims.claim: Cavity ties must be stainless steel, and a worked example with 4 millimeter round ties came out at 2.3 to 6.5 ties per square meter.
claims.source: KNB, infoblad 21

claims.claim: In one of four facade cases the inspectorate analyzed, about 80% of the old ties in a 1968 complex were rusted through, and galvanized ties often lasted less than 50 years.
claims.source: VROM-Inspectie 2007

claims.claim: Dutch facing-brick production fell from 709 million Waal-size units in 2023 to 555 million in 2024.
claims.source: KNB, Jaarverslag 2024

could_be_wrong.point: The line "Even a brick wants to be something" is credited to Louis Kahn by the press kit, but the exact wording was not found in a primary Kahn text. The piece quotes it only as the kit prints it.
could_be_wrong.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2659, Steentijd

could_be_wrong.point: How the cylinders were made and where the surplus bricks came from were not public, on the festival page, the kit or the artist's site.
The kit gives no place or date for its photos, so it is not known whether they were taken in Hall G.
could_be_wrong.source: Dutch Design Week, press kit 2659, Steentijd

could_be_wrong.point: The tie count of 2.3 to 6.5 per square meter comes from one worked example. The sheet says the structural engineer stays responsible for the real number.
The industry's own short history places the return of brick in the 12th century, while historians question early dates such as Klaarkamp and place the rise at around 1200.
The 1920s inventory calls the surviving Aduard building probably the former refectory. Some other, non-primary pages call it the infirmary.
The figure that 90% of Dutch homes have a brick facade is the trade body vice-chair's own statement, not an independent count.

glossary.plain: The Dutch word for the Stone Age. Steen is also the everyday Dutch word for a brick, so the title can also be read as brick time.
The pattern in which bricks are laid in a wall. The Dutch press kit said the cylinders showed "een nieuw verband," a new bond.
A wild bond, one of the bonds the Dutch brick makers' trade body named in its technical sheets. Van der Vleuten's 2025 work Wildverbanden took its name from it.
A kiln invented in 1858 by F.E. Hoffmann. The bricks stood in a closed loop of chambers while the fire moved from chamber to chamber, so one part heated, one fired and one cooled at the same time.
Unfired bricks. At De Werklust near Losser they dried on racks in open-air sheds before going into the kiln.
The monk's brick. The trade body's size table listed it at 280 by 105 by 80 millimeters, against 210 by 100 by 50 for the common modern Waal size.
A wall built as two parallel skins with a narrow air gap between them. From the start of the 20th century, the inner skin was the bearing wall in the main Dutch form.
A steel wire tie that holds the outer brick skin to the inner skin. The brick makers' sheet said ties must be stainless steel, and its worked example used round ties 4 millimeters across.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Eindhoven design agency Envisions opened its new studio on Hallenweg to the public for the first time, in a show called Treasured.
Its press kit listed try-outs, the Re_Work tablecloth made with the TextielMuseum, new wall lights, two guests, and hemp and wool yarns still in development.
RN Collins has no footage of the studio, so the piece reads the festival pages and press kits closely, then follows hemp and wool from plant and sheep to yarn.
start_here.how_sure_note: What the show held rests on the studio's own press kit and festival pages, with no footage and no photo of the new studio. The fiber science comes from two peer-reviewed reviews read in full, and the history from museum catalogs and the national monuments register.

claims.claim: Envisions opened its new studio at Hallenweg 1E in Eindhoven to the public for the first time during Dutch Design Week, free of charge, from 17 to 25 October 2026, 11:00 to 18:00.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Envisions," location page
claims.study: festival page, in the studio's own words

claims.claim: The show text said: "For us, true value lies not in these finished products, but in the process of creation itself."
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Treasured," programme page, DDW26

claims.claim: Every image in the 2026 press kit carries the caption "Envisions - More than this" and the credit Sanne Kaal, with no place or date, and several objects in them also appear in Dutch Design Week's 2022 photos of More Than This.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2126; Dutch Design Week Flickr, photo 52457741352
claims.study: press kit and festival photos, compared by eye

claims.claim: The kit listed "hemp and wool yarns we are currently developing as part of an Interreg project that aims to strengthen local supply chains," and named no project, partners, results or fiber mix.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2126

claims.claim: Re_Work was shown at Dutch Design Week 2025 at the Klokgebouw, hosted by the TextielMuseum; the project began in 2024, and lines woven into the cloth let it be cut into cleaning cloths without a sewing machine.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Re_Work, Envisions by TextielMuseum," programme page, DDW25

claims.claim: The Re_Work table runner is 57.8% unbleached organic cotton, 31.8% post-consumer recycled PET and 10.4% post-consumer recycled workwear.
claims.source: by TextielMuseum, "Re_Work table runner," shop page

claims.claim: A recycler in Germany turned old uniforms and plastic bottles into fibers, Spinning Jenny in Nijverdal spun them, and the yarns traveled about 150 kilometers to the TextielLab to be woven onto an organic cotton warp.
claims.source: by TextielMuseum, "New product label reveals the origin of materials used"

claims.claim: Hemp's bast fiber bundles sit in the outer stalk around a woody core of about 75% of its mass; the linen spinning machines best suited to it "have not been produced for several decades"; one ton of raw straw yields about 70 to 80 kilograms of fine long-fiber yarn.
claims.source: Zimniewska, Materials 2022

claims.claim: In 2019, hemp fiber and tow came to 60,000 tons, 0.05% of all textile fiber made worldwide.
claims.source: Zimniewska, Materials 2022

claims.claim: A wool fiber's cuticle is about 10% of its mass and its cortex about 90% of its volume; wool can hold water up to about one third of its weight and stretch up to 30% dry and 50% wet.
claims.source: Zhou et al., Animals 2025

claims.claim: An EU project page put Dutch wool at about 2.5 million kilograms a year and called it "a waste product and a cost item"; FashionUnited reported a founder's figure of about one million kilograms from about 800,000 sheep.
claims.source: EU CAP Network, Development of a sustainable value chain for Dutch wool; FashionUnited, September 2026
claims.study: EU project page and a news report of a presentation

claims.claim: A German study that blended hemp with recycled wool on a rotor spinning machine found no settings that gave the process enough stability; the yarn had many flaws and low strength but could be knitted.
claims.source: Streitenberger et al., CDATP 2024

claims.claim: In the Krimpenerwaard, hemp growing typified farming in the 16th and 17th centuries, supplied ships' rope and sails, and ended fairly suddenly with the rise of steamships.
claims.source: Plangebied vroeger en nu, WUR library
claims.study: cultural-history summary for a planning project

claims.claim: The Van der Lee rope factory in Oudewater was founded in 1545, its covered ropewalk is more than 300 meters long, and it entered the national monuments register on 10 August 2001.
claims.source: Rijksmonumentenregister, complex 517459

claims.claim: The new wall lights grew out of light objects first designed for CBRE, and the studio's online shop listed no products when checked on 1 November, after the festival.
