glossary.plain: Envisions' show at Dutch Design Week 2026, the first public opening of its new studio at Hallenweg 1E in Eindhoven, with projects, materials and try-outs, finished and in progress.
Envisions' name for its wider network of designers, each tagged by skill, such as material, textile or graphic.
A table linen range Envisions made for the TextielMuseum, begun in 2024 and first shown in 2025: tablecloths in three sizes, a table runner and fabric sold by the meter.

A label that shows which yarns are in a product and where they came from. Re_Work's had a woven QR code. An EU regulation of 13 June 2024 set up a digital version, read through a data carrier such as a barcode.
A simple historical form of damask once used for everyday table settings. Twill weaves formed its motifs, and it was cheaper than damask but just as durable.
The EU's program for cooperation between regions and countries across borders. It began in 1990, and for 2021 to 2027 almost 10 billion euros were shared among almost 100 programs.
Fiber from the outer part of a plant's stalk, not the woody center. Hemp's textile fiber is a bast fiber, held in bundles that run the whole length of the stalk.
The first step in freeing bast fiber: microbes, water, enzymes or other means break down the pectin that binds the fiber to the rest of the stalk.
The two main layers of a wool fiber: an outer sheath of overlapping scales, about 10 percent of its mass, around an inner cortex of two cell types, about 90 percent of its volume.
The natural wave in wool. One plausible explanation is the side-by-side arrangement of two kinds of cortex cell. Crimp traps air between fibers, which the review links to wool's insulation.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Noortje van Velzen showed Uitgescrolled, a social media repair café in four steps, at Sectie-C in Eindhoven.
The piece reads the press kit's route step by step and sets it beside the repair café format, the research on it and the 2025 work it grew from.
RN Collins has no footage of this work, so everything here comes from festival pages, two press kits, the designer's own site and published interviews.
start_here.how_sure_note: The four steps and their wording were checked word for word against the designer's own press kit, and the repair café figures against the foundation and a published survey paper. But nothing here was seen first hand, the award rests on the designer's own statements, and no published study shows what people took from the route.

glossary.plain: A free meeting place where people bring broken items from home and volunteers help them make the repair on the spot. The first one opened in Amsterdam in 2009.
Noortje van Velzen's project at Dutch Design Week 2026, which its press kit called a social media repair café. A printed cube in the room glossed the name as "When you're done scrolling."
The route the press kit set out, in order: Quick scan, Weigh it out, Challenge starter kit and Take it home.
The third phase. The press kit said it was filled with tips, tricks and small challenges, but it did not list the challenges.
Design that uses imagined products to point out other ways things could be. The Digital Detoxery, the 2025 work Uitgescrolled grew from, was a store of imaginary products.
In the words of a 2022 Dutch Design Week page, "the application of design methodologies to address complex human issues, prioritizing social issues."
A prize the City of Eindhoven gives once a year to a graduate in Eindhoven working on a socially relevant project. Van Velzen said she won it in 2025 with The Digital Detoxery.
Designing together with the people a project is for, usually in workshops. A 2016 introduction to social design found it among three words that kept coming back in the field.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Studio Dwarshuis showed Raw Willow: tables, bowls and candle holders of pruned branches set in what it called a bio resin.

The piece follows the branches from the pollard willow to the table, traces where Dutch landscape wood usually goes, reads the grain with the Wood Handbook and sets the resin claim against what is known about epoxy.
RN Collins has no footage of this work, so the post is built from the festival's pages, the studio's press kit and website, and published research.
start_here.how_sure_note: The facts about willow, wood structure, Dutch wood flows, epoxy and EU law come from a government handbook, a Wageningen report, peer-reviewed reviews and the official legal texts, each checked against its own words. Everything about the resin rests on the studio's short press text, which names no product and gives no test.

glossary.plain: A willow whose branches are all sawn off the head of the trunk at set intervals. In Dutch it is a knotwilg, and a Dutch guide said to cut it once every three to five years.
The studio's name for its casting resin. The studio said it was made from food-chain waste such as sugarcane bagasse, hardened with tree-derived acids. The kit named no product and gave no test.
The fibrous part of sugarcane left after the juice is pressed out. It is used as fuel in sugar mills, as animal feed and in paper.
In wood science, the preferred meaning is the direction of the long cells of the wood, as in along the grain.
A cut across the grain, the same plane that anatomy calls a cross section. Radial and tangential sections run along the grain.
The center of a stem or branch, left from its early growth before wood formed.
The reaction wood that hardwoods such as willow form on the upper side of a leaning branch, with fibers that build a jelly-like inner wall layer.
Soaking wood in furfuryl alcohol and catalysts, then heating it so the alcohol hardens inside. It is background chemistry, not the studio's stated method.
A broad green word such as environmentally friendly or biobased, with no clear and prominent specification on the same medium.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Kaustik Studio showed Strata, wool hand-tufted into layers that read like rock, at Schellens Fabriek in Eindhoven.
RN Collins has no footage of the work. The piece rests on the festival page and the press kit, whose four photos show an earlier piece, Blanco de Río.
It adds how tufting works, how geologists have read rock layers since Steno in 1669, how natural dyes are fixed to wool, and the building's past as a trijp factory.
start_here.how_sure_note: The background on tufting, geology, dyes and the building rests on patents, museum entries, a park service page and published studies, each read in full. What Strata itself looked like rests only on the studio's own text, with no published photo of the pieces.

glossary.plain: Making pile by pushing yarn through a finished backing cloth from one side, one tuft at a time.
Loop pile leaves each tuft as a closed loop. Cut pile slices the loop, so two yarn ends stand up.
Layered rocks. Each layer is also called a bed.
Steno's rule that each layer of rock is older than the one above it and younger than the one below it.
Steno's rule that layers form flat, so tilted layers were once level.
A substance, usually a metal salt, that forms a stable complex with a dye and fixes the color to the fiber.
A Dutch term for velvet made from mohair, the hair of the angora goat.
The protein that the outer, dead part of a hair is made of. Wool is a protein fiber of this kind.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, graduates of Pforzheim University in Germany showed something.beyond, in the Schellens Fabriek in Eindhoven.
The piece reads the five works the press kit named, the school's own texts on what jewelry is, and the history of the jewelry town that trained the graduates.
RN Collins has no footage of the show, so the post is built from the festival's pages, the press kit, the school's pages and the town's public documents.
start_here.how_sure_note: The town, school, museum and skin facts come from official city, school and museum pages, a university paper, an open textbook and a published review, each checked line by line. What is known about the five works themselves is thin: the kit gave only titles, makers and photo credits, with no material and no statement from any maker.

claims.claim: The BA Jewellery text said: "We understand jewellery and it's counterpart everyday objects as the dynamic relationship between material, form, body and space."

claims.claim: In 1767 a watch and jewelry factory was founded in Pforzheim's orphanage, and the city's jewelry industry grew out of it.
claims.source: Stadt Pforzheim, "Kleine Stadtchronik"

claims.claim: Around 1868 Pforzheim reached first place in European jewelry production, and in 1913, 37,500 people worked in its jewelry industry, counting home workers and people from the surrounding area.

claims.claim: The narrowly defined industry had 9,557 workers in 1949 and 22,285 in 1955, then fell to about 7,500 around 1990 and, by the author's estimate, about 1,500 in 2017.

claims.claim: The Schmuckmuseum Pforzheim called itself the world's only museum in public ownership dedicated exclusively to jewelry, with some 2,000 exhibits across five millennia.
claims.source: Schmuckmuseum Pforzheim, "The Museum" and home page

claims.source: Hochschule Pforzheim, "Project PF Revisited"

The outermost layer of the skin, usually 15 to 30 layers of dead cells deep. A ring or necklace rests on it.
The artificial canal a piercing makes through the stratum corneum. Until it heals over, the post touches immune cells in the dermis.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, textile artist Irena Egelkraut showed Rug Aya, a 2 by 3 meter hand-tufted rug of New Zealand wool and Tencel.
Its press kit said the rug began as a small sheet of paper, folded and opened again, whose creases were traced into the first sketch.
RN Collins has no footage of this work, so the piece reads the kit, the maker's own site and published research on creases, tufting, wool and lyocell.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every line was checked against its source, but the story of the rug rests only on the maker's own press kit and website, and no outside coverage was found. The science of creases and fibers comes from published studies, not from tests on Aya itself.

claims.claim: Rug Aya began as a small hand-folded paper study whose folds and traces were translated into a 2 by 3 meter textile surface of New Zealand wool and Tencel.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Rug Aya | Folds Unfolded," participant page, DDW26
claims.where: programme page lead and project text
claims.study: festival page hosted by the maker

claims.claim: The press kit said "a small sheet of paper was folded and unfolded again," that the folds "stay visible, like a memory written into the surface," and that the traces became the first sketch for the rug.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2085, "Rug Aya | Folds Unfolded"

claims.claim: The kit said Aya was hand-tufted, that New Zealand wool gave a soft and natural feel, that selected areas of Tencel added a smooth, silky feel and a subtle shine, and that different pile heights made the surface change with light, shadow and perspective.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2085, "Rug Aya | Folds Unfolded"

claims.claim: Creased Mylar sheets, pressed under a 10 kg weight for 20 minutes, relaxed to rest angles between 30 and 40 degrees whatever their thickness, which the authors tie to localized plastic deformation at the crease.

glossary.plain: A way of making pile. Yarn is pushed through a backing cloth from one side, so that loops or cut ends stand up on the other.
The two kinds of tuft one hand tufting machine can make. The pile stays a loop unless a blade cuts it.
How tall the tufts stand. The press kit said different pile heights gave Aya depth and made its surface change with light, shadow and perspective.
A sharp fold that stays. Making one bends a small zone of the sheet past the point of springing back, which physicists call localized plastic deformation.
The natural waviness of a wool fiber. With fiber diameter, it decides how wool is used.
The outer layer of a hair or wool fiber, made of thin, overlapping scales. In wool it is about 10 percent of the fiber by weight.
TENCEL is a Lenzing brand name for fibers made from wood pulp. Lyocell is made by dissolving wood pulp in a solvent and spinning it into a smooth, round fiber.
Reni Rugs' name for the white AYA colorway, the only one with Tencel accents. Pantone gave the same name to its Color of the Year for 2026.

summary: On the first Saturday of Dutch Design Week 2026, the festival listed United Cowboys' art house on Kleine Berg in Eindhoven as open from 11:00 to 18:00.
RN Collins's footage from 19:38 showed the house open and busy, and the lounge full at 19:55.
The company's own agenda explained why: it had billed that evening as the opening night of its festival program, Rough & Ready.
start_here.how_sure_note: Two details are still open, so the piece is less sure of them: which named room the hall was, and whether the canvas heap was De Grot en De Toren. The hours, the agenda and the times come from the festival's and the company's own pages and from RN Collins's own footage and photos.

ddw26-rnc-112-dusk-and-daylight-piet-hei.title: Dusk and daylight at Piet Hein Eek

summary: Piet Hein Eek's complex on Strijp-R in Eindhoven was built in the 1950s as a Philips ceramics workshop with a glass roof, and his company moved in at the end of 2010.
During Dutch Design Week 2026, RN Collins saw it at blue hour on Saturday 17 October, after sunset at 18:41, and in daylight the next afternoon.
The piece times each photo against US Naval Observatory sun data and looks at why a twilight sky stays blue.
start_here.how_sure_note: Sunset, twilight and sun heights come straight from US Naval Observatory data, and the building's history from two articles by one writer and the company's own pages. Those sources disagree on some years and on the floor area. The sky science rests on one model study and the summary of a second study.

claims.claim: On 17 October 2026 in Eindhoven, the sun set at 18:41 and civil twilight ended at 19:15.
claims.source: US Naval Observatory, "Sun and Moon data for one day," Eindhoven, 17 October 2026

claims.claim: At 19:24 the sun was 7.5 degrees below the horizon, and at 14:58 the next day it was about 25 degrees above it.
claims.source: US Naval Observatory, celestial navigation data for assumed position, Eindhoven
claims.where: computed altitude (Hc), 17:24 UT on 17 October and 12:58 UT on 18 October
claims.study: official astronomical data, geometric, without refraction

claims.claim: Civil twilight ends when the center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, and nautical twilight at 12 degrees.
claims.source: US Naval Observatory, "Rise, Set, and Twilight Definitions"

claims.claim: The building went up in the 1950s as the Philips ceramics workshop, two blocks with a street between them, under a glass roof.
claims.source: Petri Leijdekkers, "Rijke duurzaamheid. De ontwerpen van Piet Hein Eek," Ons Erfdeel 2011, no. 2

claims.claim: The company moved into the former Philips factory on Strijp-R at the end of 2010, and Eek renovated the building himself.
claims.source: Petri Leijdekkers, "Rijke duurzaamheid. De ontwerpen van Piet Hein Eek," Ons Erfdeel 2011, no. 2

claims.claim: In 1950 Philips broke ground on Strijp-R for a picture tube factory, which was torn down in 2010 to make room for homes.

claims.claim: Eek built a bar in the company restaurant from gas, water, air conditioning and heating pipes taken from the Philips factory.

claims.claim: Hulburt's 1953 paper found that with the sun at the horizon, one third of the blue overhead comes from Rayleigh scattering and two thirds from ozone absorption, and a 2023 model agreed remarkably well.
claims.source: Anna Lange, Alexei Rozanov and Christian von Savigny, "Revisiting the question 'Why is the sky blue?'," Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics 23 (2023)

claims.claim: Zenith skylight is often distinctly blue during clear civil twilights, much of it because ozone absorbs the longer wavelengths.
claims.source: Raymond L. Lee Jr., Wolfgang Meyer and Götz Hoeppe, "Atmospheric ozone and colors of the Antarctic twilight sky," Applied Optics 50, no. 28 (2011)

glossary.plain: The moment the upper edge of the sun's disk sits on the horizon. The Naval Observatory sets it at a geometric depth of 50 arcminutes for the sun's center: 16 for the disk's radius and 34 for the bending of light by the air.
The time after sunset until the center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. After it ends, artificial light is normally needed for ordinary outdoor work.
The next band after civil twilight, which ends when the center of the sun is 12 degrees below the horizon.
Sunlight scattered by the molecules of the air, the usual answer for why the sky is blue.
The parts of sunlight that ozone absorbs. With the sun at the horizon, this absorption adds to the blue of the sky overhead.
Fine particles in the air. In one twilight study, the light they took out seemed as important as ozone in explaining the sky's colors.
The Dutch word for a television picture tube, the part Philips made at a factory on Strijp-R that was torn down in 2010.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the studio Atelier Fig. served a breakfast by Atelier Nori inside its show at Hallenweg 11 in Eindhoven, listed from 09:30 to 11:00.
RN Collins, invited by the studio, reached the door at 10:55. The hosts fed her anyway, and she stayed until about 11:33.
The piece follows that morning into a study of open kitchens, what Michelin stars leave out and the Dutch word gastvrij.
start_here.how_sure_note: The times and events of the morning come from RN Collins's own photos and footage, and the research is quoted from the study, the guide and the dictionary. The open-kitchen result comes from one dining hall with silent screens, so it does not test a room like this one, where staff and guests talked.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Tante Netty turned Museum van de WWij, a 33 square meter neighborhood museum in Woensel-West, Eindhoven, into a peep box.
Its host said the name means Museum of Us, with a second W for Woensel-West, the neighborhood once called the city's problem area.
The show's pun on muse and amuse leads to the Greek root of every museum, and a bust on a column leads back to Vitruvius.
start_here.how_sure_note: The history, numbers and word origins come from registers, statistics, dictionaries and the festival's own pages. The meaning of the name rests on the host's words on tape, and most objects in the room have no confirmed maker.

glossary.plain: The Dutch pronoun for we, a word related to English we.
Dutch for peep box, a box you look into through holes. DDW's Dutch text called the museum een grote kijkdoos, a big peep box.
An older Dutch word for a sort of peep show, first found in 1709, from raar, strange, and kieken, to look.
A word coined in French in 1822 by the painter Louis Daguerre, from Greek roots meaning through and spectacle. Later the Dutch word came to mean a peep-box show.
In Dutch restaurants, a small bite served with the aperitif, from the French amuse-gueule.
One of the nine Muses of Greek myth, goddesses of the arts and sciences. From 1575 the French word muse could also mean an artist's source of inspiration.
From Greek Mouseion, first a place where the Muses were worshipped. By its roots, a house of the Muses.
The top of an Ionic column, with two spirals called volutes. Vitruvius said they hung at the right and left like curly ringlets.

summary: Plug-in City, a village of sea containers on Strijp-S, a former Philips factory district in Eindhoven, hosted shows at Dutch Design Week 2026.
Innovation Origins reported that it started in 2014, and in December 2017 it reported a planned move of about 500 meters for early 2018.
Containers can be stacked, lent and moved because the shipping world agreed on one shape. The group's own site says: "Nothing is permanent."
start_here.how_sure_note: The Philips history, the monument, the prize and the container story come from official pages, a national register, a historian and a published essay. The village's own history rests on 2017 press reports and the group's site, and no source read says whether the planned move took place.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Luca Ortmann's Waiting for the Bus put yellow steel rails, lamps and a small table on the Demer, a shopping street in Eindhoven.
The work began as a 2025 bachelor's project at UdK Berlin, aimed at the temporary replacement bus stop.
The Demer was bombed in 1942, rebuilt and repaved, and the textbook shows where a waiting body's weight goes when it stands or sits.
start_here.how_sure_note: No source gives the pieces' heights, and no study has measured anyone using them, so the piece makes no claim about what they do for the body. The project facts come from DDW's and the school's own pages, the street's history from city documents, and the anatomy from a textbook.
start_here.how_sure_approved: RN approved Nov 24: how sure set from "strong" to "moderate"; note rewritten in plain words to give the reason

summary: Burgers, a building in Eindhoven, was squatted in 1990 and bought by its residents in 1992, by their own written history and the Dutch Design Week page.
On the morning of October 17, 2026, Lele and Rens of The Purple Show were still building the stand for their sign there, before the doors opened.
The piece sets the residents' history beside a resident's account on tape, Dutch squatting law and European figures on textile waste.
start_here.how_sure_note: The dates, the law and the textile figures come from official pages, and the morning comes from RN's own footage. Much of the building's story rests only on the residents' own history and one resident on tape, and their counts of homes and workshops do not match.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Electric Grand by Antoon Versteegde and Bart van Dongen gave every key of a Yamaha CP-70 electric grand its own speaker, hung in a bamboo frame.
The CP-70 kept real strings and hammers and had a pickup for each key, which made the split possible.
The piece then turns to the outer ear, the body part shaped to collect sound from the air.
start_here.how_sure_note: The work is described from the festival's and the makers' own pages, and no independent review was found. The instrument comes from a museum and from Yamaha, and the ear from two anatomy textbooks. Who played at about 15:00 is not known.

claims.claim: Electric Grand: Walk inside a Piano is by the visual artist Antoon Versteegde and the pianist and composer Bart van Dongen, and every key has its own dedicated speaker and its own volume control, hung in a light bamboo structure.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Electric Grand: Walk inside a Piano," program page, DDW26 archive

claims.claim: Live performances alternated with times when people explored the sound on their own.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Electric Grand: Walk inside a Piano," program page, DDW26 archive

claims.claim: Each key of the Yamaha CP-70 is routed to its own channel and individual speaker, and the electronics were rebuilt in recent years by Fontys InnovationLab.
claims.source: Electric Grand, home page

claims.claim: Yamaha's CP-70 and CP-80 came onto the market in 1976; the CP-70 has 73 keys, and a separate piezo pickup was fitted for each key.
claims.source: SMEM, "Yamaha CP-70B," collection page

claims.claim: The CP-70 was developed to give the expression of an acoustic piano while holding its own on stage next to electric guitars at full volume.
claims.source: Yamaha Corporation, "CP-70," Innovation Road display collection

claims.claim: The first try-out took place on August 21, 2021, at Theaterfestival Boulevard in 's-Hertogenbosch, and the Eindhoven run of October 17 to 25, 2026 was called its definitive presentation.
claims.source: Electric Grand, home page; Theaterfestival Boulevard, "Electric Grand," program page, 2021
claims.study: the makers' own site and a festival program page

claims.claim: Cage tried a pie plate and then nails on the strings, and found that screws or bolts would stay in position.
claims.source: John Cage, "How the Piano Came to be Prepared," John Cage Trust, archived copy

claims.claim: The auricula projects from the side of the head and serves to collect the vibrations of the air; the canal runs about 2.5 cm from the bottom of the concha to the eardrum in an S-shaped curve.
claims.source: Henry Gray, Anatomy of the Human Body (1918), "The External Ear"

claims.claim: The C-shaped curves of the auricle direct sound waves toward the auditory canal.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 14.1, "Sensory Perception"

ddw26-rnc-133-park-on-the-flat-roofs.title: A park on the flat roofs

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, visitors at Stadslab Eindhoven built a park in LEGO, upside down on the ceiling of the Upside Park room.
Upside Park is a city idea for green, public parks on the many flat roofs of Eindhoven's 1950s post-war homes.
The festival said the city intends to use those roofs for greenery, but no source found describes a plan, budget figure or council decision for a public roof park.
start_here.how_sure_note: What the festival and the city project said comes from their own pages, and the room comes from RN Collins's own footage. Whether a roof park will be built is not known: no plan was found, and a missing plan is hard to prove. The green-roof count comes from a study by two advocacy groups, not a government count.

claims.claim: Between autumn 2024 and summer 2025, 8,000 ideas were collected with the help of 40 partners, and in autumn 2025 they were filtered into six city goals, one of them a greener Eindhoven.

claims.claim: Eindhoven possesses a relatively large number of flat roofs on homes from the post-war reconstruction period (1950s), and the municipality intends to utilize these to create more greenery in the city.

ddw26-rnc-201-palm-sized-camera.title: Five rules for filming a design week

summary: At her first Dutch Design Week, in 2026, RN Collins filmed makers, guides and a press tour on a palm-sized camera with two clip-on wireless mics.
Her footage shows five working rules: ask before you mic, hand over the second mic, get their actual words, point the camera at them, and film the room.
The piece sets those rules beside the Dutch press council's guideline and studies of how speech to text can mishear or invent words.
start_here.how_sure_note: The scenes and quotes come from RN Collins's own footage, checked against the studio's soundbite list. The press guideline, the act and the speech studies were read in full. The 40 percent figure comes from a 1991 news report, not the study itself, and the guideline is quoted in the writer's own translation from Dutch.

claims.claim: The Dutch press council's guideline says journalists make themselves known as journalists and tell people enough about the publication to make an informed choice about taking part.
claims.source: Raad voor de Journalistiek, Leidraad, version of September 2026

claims.claim: The guideline says quotes from interviews may not be used in a different context from the one the person could expect.
claims.source: Raad voor de Journalistiek, Leidraad, version of September 2026

claims.claim: A study reported in 1991 found that 40 percent of the quotes from the 1984 presidential debates in national publications' reports were less than word for word.
claims.source: Deseret News, "Is misquoting common in journalism?", January 15, 1991
claims.study: secondary news report of a study by Adrienne Lehrer

claims.claim: Whisper was trained on 680,000 hours of audio and transcripts collected from the internet and came close to human accuracy on standard tests.
claims.source: Radford et al., "Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision," arXiv:2212.04356, 2022

claims.claim: In a test of 13,140 short audio segments, roughly 1 percent of Whisper transcriptions held whole phrases or sentences not in the audio, and 38 percent of those passages included explicit harms.
claims.source: Koenecke et al., "Careless Whisper," arXiv:2402.08021v2, 2024

claims.claim: Five commercial speech recognition systems had an average word error rate of 0.35 for Black speakers and 0.19 for white speakers.
claims.source: Koenecke et al., "Racial disparities in automated speech recognition," PNAS 117(14), 2020
claims.study: peer-reviewed study of 42 white and 73 Black speakers

claims.source: Uitvoeringswet Algemene verordening gegevensbescherming, article 43

summary: In October 2026, RN Collins flew from Hawaii to the Netherlands for the first time, for her first design week of any kind, where she knew no one in person.
She had found Dutch Design Week by searching online, and she came as accredited press for the Journal of Biophilic Design.
The piece sets her own taped words beside what the festival was: its 26th edition, nine days in Eindhoven, on a former Philips site.
start_here.how_sure_note: Her words are quoted from checked transcripts of her own footage, and the trip facts come from her own notes. The festival facts come from the organizer's own pages and the national monument register. One staff member's remark is described, not quoted, because only one machine transcript holds it.

summary: On Saturday, October 17, 2026, RN Collins planned a short talk with the makers of The Purple Show at Burgers in Eindhoven and stayed a little over two hours.
That night she called the morning the best part of her day. The next day she compared it with other interviews, which the piece does not name.

summary: On two press tours at Dutch Design Week 2026, RN Collins filmed a guide's instruction, a question about who paid for a neighborhood museum and a question about trees at a hornet trap.
In each case the first answer said what something was, and a second question from the group said more about the place or the problem.
The piece then follows the second question through medical teaching, a Toyota factory rule and studies of conversation, including where it can go wrong.
start_here.how_sure_note: What was said on the tours comes from RN Collins's own footage, mostly as paraphrase, with the few quoted lines checked word for word. The teaching research is solid on how teachers ask, but reviews call much of the evidence for the teaching models low to moderate in quality.

glossary.plain: A five-step way to teach in five minutes or less: get a commitment, probe for supporting evidence, teach general rules, reinforce what was done right, and correct mistakes.
The second step of that model: after a first answer, the teacher asks what evidence supports it, or what else was considered.
Six steps for a student presenting a case, one of which hands the questions to the learner: probe the teacher about what is uncertain.
The pause between a question and an answer. A few extra seconds led to longer answers and more follow-up questions.
Explaining to yourself why a stated fact or idea is true, by asking why.
Failing to keep weighing other reasonable answers once a first diagnosis is reached.
Taiichi Ohno's rule at Toyota: ask why about a problem five times, so the last answer goes deeper than the first.

safety.note: This piece covers design tours, teaching research and conversation studies and gives no medical guidance.

summary: On Saturday 17 October 2026, at The Purple Show in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week, RN Collins filmed a harness woven from old bicycle inner tubes being tried on.
The work was INTERLOOM by Josquin Fromangé. The designer's card describes modules such as pouches that can be added or removed.
The piece then follows where inner tubes came from, how a weave holds together and the shoulder bones a harness sits on.
start_here.how_sure_note: What the work is rests on the designer's own printed card, one award entry and RN Collins's own footage, and no other source on the work was found. The tire history and the anatomy come from a national museum and an open textbook. No source says how the harness carries load or whether it is comfortable.

Built from parts that can be added, removed or replaced. The card says pouches can be added or removed to suit personal needs.
The process of interlacing strands or strips of various materials. Strips count as well as threads.
A simple criss-cross checkerboard pattern, where strands pass over and under two or more others.
A tire that rides on a cushion of pressurized air. Robert William Thomson invented the first one in 1845.
The clavicle and the scapula, which attach the arm to the breastbone.
The collarbone. The only long bone that lies in a horizontal position in the body, and the most commonly fractured bone.
A dislocation of the joint at the tip of the shoulder, often after a strong blow to the side of the shoulder.

summary: At Class of 26, Hasan Alp Celikel showed a guitar, glasses and shoes made for one body.
Celikel says the guitar fits their proportions and playing, and the glasses and shoes came from VR and body scans.
The piece follows each object to the body part it meets: the hands, the face and the foot.

summary: Teun Zwets's Splitted furniture starts with splitting wooden beams with an axe, and the cracks and grain stay visible under the lacquer.
Wood opens along its grain because its long cells part far more easily than they break.
Anatomists also follow planes already in the body, the layers called fascia. The comparison is this piece's own and holds only up to a point.
start_here.how_sure_note: The wood science comes from a government handbook and a peer-reviewed paper, and the maker's method from the festival and Dezeen. The speaker at the museum very likely meant Teun Zwets, but the name on the tape is uncertain, and the link between wood and the body is this piece's own comparison.

glossary.plain: The face exposed when a log is split exactly from pith to bark.
A long, thin wood cell. In softwoods such as fir, tracheids make up more than 90% of the wood's volume.
A band of brick-shaped cells running from the pith out to the bark, like the spokes of a wheel.
Having different mechanical properties along three directions at right angles: along the grain, across the growth rings and along them.
A sheath, sheet or other layer of connective tissue that can be dissected, and that attaches, encloses and separates muscles and organs.
The sheath of connective tissue around a whole skeletal muscle, which lets the muscle move on its own.
A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped by a layer called the perimysium. The word comes from Latin for a little bundle.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the student collective Het Beun Collectief showed Heavy Metals, a show about metal, in its Eindhoven workshop.
Three steel machine parts on a bench held candles. No source names them, and the piece reads them as tool holders from the photo.
The show's text said society built itself with a spine of metals, a phrase the piece follows into coins, candlesticks and bones.

summary: At a stone studio in Eindhoven, someone on the press tour asked if the window was all ceramics, and the designer said, "No, stone."
Marble is limestone or dolostone changed by heat and pressure in the earth, and travertine is calcite laid down by springs and rivers.
Ceramic is clay that people shape and then change for good in a kiln, and fired clay has passed for stone for some 250 years.
start_here.how_sure_note: The definitions of marble, travertine and ceramic come from museum, survey and textbook sources that agree. The scene rests on RN Collins's own footage, and no object in the window was tested.

could_be_wrong.point: The piece does not say which object in the window was which stone. The words "some ceramics" on the same clip suggest the window may have held both, and the question itself is not quoted because the transcripts do not agree on it.
The piece does not say where Kiwano's red stone was quarried or what a lab would call it. A trade name such as Rosso Levanto marble can name a rock that geologists do not call marble.
could_be_wrong.source: Oxford University Museum of Natural History, Corsi collection, stone 484

could_be_wrong.point: Kiwano's own page says only that its rough forms come from different regions of Turkey, so the piece does not tie its stone to Denizli. The 2006 figure on Turkey's share of US travertine is old, and the market has shifted since.

None of the clues for telling stone from ceramic is proof. The acid and scratch tests leave damage, a glaze can mislead a water test, and the tap test checks whether a block is sound, not what it is made of.

ddw26-rnc-226-wide-lens-nose.title: Why your selfies make your nose look bigger

summary: A close camera makes the nose look bigger because the nose is much nearer the lens than the ears are.
The anatomy stays the same. Camera position sets the perspective, and the lens sets how much of the scene fits.
A 2018 model put the effect at about 30 percent wider from 12 inches, for average faces.
start_here.how_sure_note: The geometry is well established in physics texts and a forensic review. The 30 percent comes from one model of average faces, and studies of real faces match it only in part.

claims.source: Ward B, Ward M, Fried O, Paskhover B, "Nasal distortion in short-distance photographs: the selfie effect," JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery 20, no. 4 (2018): 333 to 335

summary: The outer ear is built from two materials: one folded plate of elastic cartilage above and a soft lobe below.
The lobe has no cartilage. It is made of connective tissue and fat.
Engineers have tried to grow ears from scratch, and matching the material has been harder than matching the shape. This is anatomy, not piercing or medical advice.
start_here.how_sure_note: The basic anatomy is long settled and agrees across Gray, a modern textbook and two recent reviews. The tissue engineering is younger, and some of those papers were read as abstracts only.

Rens described days of about 13 hours during the build, and both makers work with second-hand, deadstock and thrifted cloth.

summary: On October 19, 2026, at Dutch Design Week, Cities of Things presented a manifesto of ten considerations for AI that works in rooms and streets.
In the workshop that followed, teams built carts on hoverboards and plywood, and a person steered each one by radio.
In the same building, a second show and its handbook asked who decides how such technology is used, and how residents can keep talking back to it.
start_here.how_sure_note: The manifesto, handbook and study lines are quoted or closely matched to the documents. What happened that afternoon comes from RN Collins's own footage, partly as paraphrase. The manifesto's claims about where AI is going are the maker's view, not tested findings, and its pages give slightly different counts of experts and years.

claims.claim: The manifesto opens: "We are entering an era in which artificial intelligence leaves the screen and enters the room."
claims.source: Cities of Things, "Cities of Things Manifesto"

claims.claim: The manifesto groups ten considerations in five clusters: legibility interplay, intelligence is humble, design honesty, support community and provide openness.
claims.source: Cities of Things, "Cities of Things Manifesto"; RN Collins, own footage, Monday 19 October 2026

summary: On Monday, October 19, 2026, RN Collins joined a Cities of Things workshop at Dutch Design Week, sat at one team's table for part of the afternoon and filmed the rest.
Each table got a fixed, imagined 2050 future from a TU Delft study, a set of driver cards and a tray of LEGO, and one table built Happy Glasses, a design fiction.
The piece follows the method step by step and traces it to scenario work, the futures cone and design fiction, keeping every claim about 2050 with the people who made it.
start_here.how_sure_note: What happened at the table comes from RN Collins's own footage and photos, with the few quoted lines checked word for word. The 2050 futures are imagined scenarios, and their own authors say they are not predictions. The glasses were never tested.

summary: At a Cities of Things workshop at Dutch Design Week 2026, a talk slide listed Social Credit System as one possible force in an imagined future.
Within the hour, one table, where RN Collins sat for part of the workshop, sketched glasses that give the wearer social points for reporting litter.
The piece stays inside that design exercise and asks what research on rewards, clean streets and face-worn cameras says about each part of the idea.
start_here.how_sure_note: The workshop lines come from RN Collins's own footage and photos, with the quotes checked word for word. The research is mostly solid lab and field work, but several papers were read only as abstracts, and none of them tested glasses like these.

claims.claim: A 2019 review of 819 studies found gamification results leaned positive, with a remarkable amount of mixed results.
claims.source: Koivisto J, Hamari J, International Journal of Information Management 45 (2019)

claims.claim: Rewards for taking part, finishing or doing well lowered free-choice intrinsic motivation (effect sizes -0.40, -0.36 and -0.28), while positive feedback raised it.
claims.source: Deci EL, Koestner R, Ryan RM, Psychological Bulletin 125, no. 6 (1999)

claims.claim: In a parking garage, 139 people littered more on a littered floor than a clean one, 41% against 11%, and 54% against 6% after watching a helper drop litter.
claims.source: Cialdini RB, Reno RR, Kallgren CA, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 58, no. 6 (1990)

claims.claim: A 2021 replication with 1,798 participants found less littering in clean places, but a single piece of litter in a clean place led to as much littering as a fully littered place.
claims.source: Bergquist M et al., Journal of Environmental Psychology 74 (2021)
claims.study: two pre-registered field experiments and one online experiment

claims.claim: At the time of its 2020 preprint, the TACO litter dataset held 1,500 images with 4,784 annotations, and most cigarette annotations covered less than 64 by 64 pixels.
claims.source: Proença PF, Simões P, arXiv 2003.06975 (2020)

claims.claim: Of 31 people interviewed near mock camera glasses in cafés, 17 said they would prefer to be asked before being filmed.
claims.source: Denning T, Dehlawi Z, Kohno T, CHI 2014

claims.claim: For a well-liked charity, unpaid students pressed about 822 key pairs in public and about 548 in private; pay raised private effort to about 740 while public effort fell to about 702, a change the authors found not significant.
claims.source: Ariely D, Bracha A, Meier S, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston Working Paper 07-9 (2007)

claims.claim: A 2018 meta-analysis of 117 papers found a small but significant positive link between being observed and acting for others, stronger with real observers and in the laboratory.
claims.source: Bradley AP, Lawrence C, Ferguson E, Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2018)

claims.claim: The Cities of Things manifesto says that communities define the kind of environment they want before agentic systems are introduced.
claims.source: Cities of Things, "Cities of Things Manifesto"

could_be_wrong.point: TACO is a preprint, and its authors wrote that it still needed many more annotations before it could support reliable litter detection in the wild.

summary: On October 19, 2026, at Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, plywood carts built in a Cities of Things workshop crossed a brick square, each steered by a person with a radio remote.
The cart's build page, its open firmware and the radio's manual, read together, point to one stick doing the driving, under one thumb.
The piece then reads that thumb: its two bones, the saddle joint at its base, the four muscles in its pad and the long tendons from the forearm.
start_here.how_sure_note: The anatomy comes from standard textbooks and is well settled. Which stick drove each cart is a working answer from three documents and two close frames, because no frame shows how the radios were set.

claims.source: Flysky, FS-i6 User Manual (2016)

claims.claim: The hand has 27 bones: eight carpals, five metacarpals and 14 phalanges, and the thumb has two phalanges where each finger has three.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 8.2

claims.claim: The joint between the trapezium and the first metacarpal is a saddle joint, and its movement gives humans their opposable thumbs.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 9.4

claims.claim: Four thenar muscles form the pad at the base of the thumb: abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis and adductor pollicis.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 11.5

claims.claim: Opponens pollicis moves the thumb across the palm to touch the other fingers, and it is the one muscle in the pad that inserts on the first metacarpal itself.

claims.claim: Abductor pollicis brevis is supplied by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve in 95% of people, by the ulnar nerve in 2.5% and by both in 2%.
claims.source: Bouredoucen H et al., RöFo 198, no. 4 (2026): 457 to 478

claims.claim: Extensor pollicis brevis and extensor pollicis longus each extend the thumb, and abductor pollicis longus also extends it.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 11.5

claims.claim: De Quervain tenosynovitis is an overuse condition of the sheath of the first extensor compartment of the wrist, and its exact cause is unknown.
claims.source: Challoumas D et al., JAMA Network Open 6, no. 10 (2023): e2337001

claims.claim: In 1956, Napier named the two basic patterns of the hand's movements precision grip and power grip.
claims.source: Napier JR, Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British) 38-B, no. 4 (1956): 902 to 913

could_be_wrong.point: No frame from the day shows a settings screen, and a stick mode is chosen in the radio's menus. The one-stick reading comes from the build page, the firmware and the manual together, plus two close frames of a thumb on one stick.
The build page names more than one radio and does not say which model each cart used on the day.
None of the sources says which muscle works when a thumb pushes a stick in a given direction. That would take a measurement, and none was found.

No study found in this research tested whether steering a cart, or using any two-stick transmitter, affects the first compartment of the wrist. The cause of de Quervain tenosynovitis is unknown, and whether inflammation plays a part is still argued.
could_be_wrong.source: Challoumas D et al., JAMA Network Open 6, no. 10 (2023): e2337001

could_be_wrong.point: Anatomists have not always counted the thumb's bones the same way. In 1833, Bell wrote that the thumb has no metacarpal bone; modern texts give it one, the first.
Napier's two grips were read only in his numbered summary, which does not discuss a hand on a stick, so how a transmitter grip fits them is left open.
could_be_wrong.source: Napier JR, Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British) 1956

glossary.plain: The soft, rounded pad at the base of the thumb, formed by four small muscles that all act on the thumb.
A joint where both surfaces curve in on one side and out on the other, so the bones fit like a rider on a saddle.
Bringing the tip of the thumb to the tip of a finger, made by a mix of flexion and abduction at the saddle joint.
Intrinsic muscles start and end inside the hand; extrinsic muscles start in the forearm and reach the hand by long tendons.
The hollow on the thumb side of the wrist that shows when the thumb is straightened hard, with the radial artery crossing its floor.
An overuse condition of the sheath in the first tunnel on the back of the wrist, which holds two of the thumb's tendons.
A radio transmitter setting, chosen in its menus, that decides what each stick does.
Pinching an object between the fingers and the opposing thumb, or clamping it between the bent fingers and the palm.

summary: At a Cities of Things workshop during Dutch Design Week 2026, small tables got a future already written, named the forces in it, built an object in LEGO and presented it.
RN Collins, an anatomist and medical educator, joined one table for part of the afternoon and filmed the rest.
The piece sets those four steps beside the way medicine has taught from cases since 1900, and reports what education research has and has not shown about each one.
start_here.how_sure_note: The history is solid: Cannon's and Cabot's own words were read on scans of the original pages. The workshop steps come from RN Collins's own footage, mostly as paraphrase. The research shows learners enjoy case teaching, but its edge over other active methods is still unsettled, and the LEGO studies are small and short term.

could_be_wrong.point: A 2012 review of 104 studies found the evidence on case-based learning's effects, compared with other activities, inconclusive. Against other active methods, such as design thinking, small studies found no clear winner.
The preference study at two California schools measured what students and faculty liked, and its authors say it could not show which method produces better doctors.
The LEGO session in Dublin had no control group, volunteer students and a test straight after, so it cannot show lasting effects. The clay review found no evidence of long-term gains.
The 2025 meta-analysis on standardized patients rated the certainty of its knowledge and practice results as low, because results varied from trial to trial.
Several papers were read only as abstracts because the full text was behind a paywall, including Barrows 1993, Sturdy 2007, Srinivasan 2007 and Thistlethwaite 2012.

glossary.plain: Teaching from authentic cases, where students and teachers both prepare ahead and the talk is guided so the main points get covered.
Students get little advance preparation and little direction, and learn as the case unfolds.
In Cannon's plan, the meeting where one student states the case and others analyze the symptoms, give the differential points and suggest treatment, while the rest judge what they hear.
A well person trained to act out an illness the same way each time, or a real patient trained to present their own illness that way.
Maastricht's seven-step sequence for a problem: clarify terms, define the problem, brainstorm, sort the explanations, set learning goals, study them and report back.
A six-step format for a student presenting a case, built so the student says their reasoning and their doubts out loud.
The standard pose anatomists describe the body in: upright, with the toes and palms facing forward, whatever way the body actually lies.
At the workshop, the forces shaping a future, sorted into five groups: societal and cultural, political, nature, economic and technological.

summary: On October 19, 2026, at a Cities of Things workshop during Dutch Design Week, two plywood Wijkbot carts were each steered by a person with a radio, and RN Collins filmed the build, the lift and the street test.
The piece then follows the people behind other machines: a hidden chess player, a driver in a car seat costume, remote helpers for robotaxis and the workers who plot routes for delivery robots.
It ends with a 2018 Dutch law that treats the person outside a test vehicle as its driver and asks each permit to say who and where that driver is.
start_here.how_sure_note: The workshop lines come from RN Collins's own footage, with the quotes checked word for word. The robotaxi figures are the companies' own statements, the Markey report is one senator's oversight document, and two of the studies were read only as abstracts.

A test in which a hidden person does the work that people think a machine is doing. J. F. Kelley named it the OZ paradigm in 1984.
Help from a person far away who answers questions sent by a self-driving car. At Waymo, the car's own driving system stays in control.
A point on a route. For Kiwibots, people in Colombia plotted waypoints and the robots drove the short hops between them.

Under a 2018 Dutch law, the person steering a test vehicle from outside it counts as its driver, and each permit must say who that driver is and where.

summary: On Monday 19 October 2026, RN Collins filmed a Cities of Things workshop in Eindhoven, where plywood Wijkbot carts were driven by people with radio remotes.
The next day, a free Physical AI track at the TechEx expo in Amsterdam put autonomy and robot fleets in its titles. RN did not go, so that side comes only from the published program.
The piece sets the two rooms side by side and follows one question, who is controlling it, through Tesla's 1898 boat, open-source robot arms, company accounts and EU law.
start_here.how_sure_note: The Eindhoven side rests on RN Collins's own footage, with the quoted lines checked against the tape. The Amsterdam side is only what the program said each session would cover, and the Waymo, 1X and Capgemini facts are each company's own account.

glossary.plain: A neighborhood robot from a Cities of Things kit: a plywood deck on a hacked second-hand hoverboard, steered by a person with a radio remote.
A test in which a person plays the robot, driving it and speaking for it, while others react to it.
A person driving or moving a robot from a distance.
A person moves one arm, the leader, and a second arm, the follower, copies it.
A name suggested in Tesla's time for the art of controlling the movements and operations of distant machines.
Tesla's phrase for his remote-controlled machines: each one was part of the distant operator who sent it orders.
Waymo's name for staff who give advice and support to its self-driving system but do not steer or drive the car.
In the EU machinery law, machines that move and whose safety functions work without an operator always at the controls.
Under the same law, a way for a person to get information from a distance and stop, start or move an autonomous machine to a safe spot.

summary: A sign at Dutch Design Week 2026 said "40% of global soils are degraded. Due to intensive farming practices." It named no source.
The closest UN figure is up to 40 percent of the world's land, the top of a 20 to 40 percent range. A 2000 farm study put 42.9 percent of its own farm map in map units with moderate soil damage.
No source found for this piece says 40 percent of the world's soils are degraded because of intensive farming. Farming practices were one cause among several on the 1990 world soil map.
start_here.how_sure_note: Each figure is quoted word for word from the report that published it, and most were read in full. The estimates themselves vary a lot, because experts, satellites and national reports count degraded land in different ways.

glossary.plain: The thing a percentage is a share of. Change it and the same number means something different.
The lasting decline or loss of soil, water and living things on a piece of land. Soil is one part of land.
Soil pressed denser by weight at the surface, with fewer large pores, so roots, water and air move through it less easily.
The Global Assessment of Human-Induced Soil Degradation: a world map of soil damage published in 1990, drawn from the opinions of soil experts.
The 2000 study's own map of where farming happens. It includes areas that are up to 70 percent non-agricultural.
One area on a soil map that gets a single label, even when only part of it is degraded.
The dark top layer of soil. It takes around a thousand years to form just a few centimetres of it.
Soil whose density and pore space fall past set threshold values in a measured test.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, TERRA FIRMA by Judith Sanders showed black pumps on heels of weathered oak, painted with find numbers, in the EX SITU show.
The show says the oak came from a Roman road in South Holland, and its adviser called the work in fact illegal under Dutch law.
The piece checks those claims against a 2025 inspector's report, tree-ring entries and the depot's own rules, and asks what a higher heel does to the foot.
start_here.how_sure_note: The rule on keeping finds, the survey figures and the tree-ring entries come from official documents read in full. Where these heels' wood came from rests only on the show's own words, and the age of the sneaker's leather is disputed.

claims.claim: Two numbers were painted on the TERRA FIRMA pumps, 7144 and 7074, and the show's adviser told the press tour they were the archaeologists' find numbers, each tied to a GPS location.
claims.source: RN Collins, own footage (DJI Osmo Nano) and iPhone photos, Saturday 17 October 2026, EX SITU stop, Klokgebouw
claims.where: card 02 clip c0007, shot log; iPhone photos 14:23 to 14:29 CEST
claims.study: own footage; the adviser is not named on tape

claims.claim: The festival page says the wood is "Oak from the Roman Limes road (125 AD) built under Emperor Hadrian," excavated in South Holland and deselected for museum collections or further research.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "TERRA FIRMA," participant page, DDW26
claims.where: page intro, read from a saved copy of 19 October 2026

claims.claim: EX SITU gave nine designer-artists deselected archaeological finds excavated in South Holland, and the full show was planned for See Lab in The Hague from 5 February to 7 March 2027.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "EX SITU: Matter in Translation," program page, DDW26
claims.where: program page, read from a saved copy of 19 October 2026

claims.claim: The adviser said the work was in fact illegal under Dutch law. The inspector's 2025 report says instead that the Heritage Act requires keeping all archaeological finds from excavations.
claims.source: Inspectie Overheidsinformatie en Erfgoed, "Van vondst tot vuilnis," 2025
claims.where: PDF p. 1 (cover); the adviser's words from RN Collins's footage

claims.claim: The inspector's report rests on a survey of 49 excavation firms and services and 37 depots, run in 2023 and 2024, plus field visits.
claims.source: Inspectie Overheidsinformatie en Erfgoed, "Van vondst tot vuilnis," 2025

claims.claim: Thirty-seven percent of firms said they destroy all finds that do not go to a depot; 2 percent of destinations were an art object.
claims.source: Inspectie Overheidsinformatie en Erfgoed, "Van vondst tot vuilnis," 2025

claims.claim: Fifteen of the 41 firms that set finds aside after the field keep neither a closer identification, a photo nor a drawing of them.
claims.source: Inspectie Overheidsinformatie en Erfgoed, "Van vondst tot vuilnis," 2025

claims.claim: The minister sent the report to parliament on 2 February 2026 and said it would be weighed in the work on changes to the Heritage Act. As of that letter, the rule on keeping every find had not changed.
claims.source: Minister of Education, Culture and Science (G. Moes), letter to the House of Representatives, Kamerstuk 32 820, no. 564, 2 February 2026

claims.claim: The South Holland depot asks for every find number to come with its material, its type and the numbers of its trench, level, soil feature and drawing.
claims.source: Provinciaal Depot Bodemvondsten Zuid-Holland, "Voorwaarden aanlevering vondsten," conditions for handing over finds

claims.claim: A public tree-ring entry for oak piles of the Roman road at Valkenburg has a dated ring series running up to AD 124, a ring-end year, not a felling year.
claims.source: Doeve P (BAAC bv), "Dendrochronologisch onderzoek Romeinse weg traject Valkenburg Rijnlandroute-Tjalmastrook (BAAC project 19.0302)," DataverseNL, 2019
claims.where: entry metadata; report and ring files restricted

claims.claim: Wood used to build a road along the limes in the Netherlands was felled in a single season, AD 124 to 125, from woodland between the Rhine and the Meuse.
claims.source: Visser RM, "Relating Roman Rings," PhD thesis, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, 2025, public abstract

claims.claim: In 35 women tested in sneakers and in 2-inch and 3-inch heels, pressure under the forefoot rose significantly as the heel got higher.
claims.source: Mandato MG, Nester E, "The effects of increasing heel height on forefoot peak pressure," Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association 89, no. 2 (1999): 75 to 80

claims.claim: A review of 81 studies with 1,501 participants found an anterior shift in plantar pressure in high heels, meaning pressure under the sole moved forward.
claims.source: Zeng Z, Liu Y, Hu X, Li P, Wang L, "Effects of high-heeled shoes on lower extremity biomechanics and balance in females," BMC Public Health 23 (2023): 726

glossary.plain: The working label an excavation gives each find. In South Holland the depot asks for each find number to come with its material, its type and the numbers of its trench, level, soil feature and drawing.
Setting aside excavated finds so they are not kept in a depot. The 2025 inspector's report studied how often this happens and where those finds go.
A store where excavated finds are kept with their excavation documents and reports. The Netherlands has 38 of them.
Out of the ground, or out of its original place. The inspector's report uses it for finds and knowledge that can be lost after a dig.
The Roman frontier along the Rhine. Part of it, the Lower German Limes, became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021.
The last dated tree ring in a sample. It is not the same as the year the tree was cut down.
The heel bone, the largest bone of the foot.
The front of the foot, where the heads of the five metatarsal bones rest on the ground.

law_policy.status: Finds from an excavation with no proven owner belong to the province, a city with a designated depot, or the state, and are stored in depots with their documents. Version in force from 22 November 2025.
The minister sent the inspector's report to parliament on 2 February 2026; any change on deselection was to be weighed in work on the Heritage Act. As of that letter, the rule had not changed.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the Dutch furniture brand Planq showed Bakkie, a stacking chair whose shell is made with dried coffee grounds and recycled plastic.
Planq set out the recipe on four printed cards: coffee, dried grounds, recycled plastic and a blended granulate that is molded into the shell.
Research on coffee-filled plastics backs the card's split of the work, but Planq gives no weight or share for the coffee, only a figure of 50 espressos per chair.
start_here.how_sure_note: What the chair is made of comes from Planq's own cards and pages and RN Collins's photos. The science comes from lab studies of other coffee composites, not tests of this chair, and how much of the shell is coffee is not known.

claims.claim: Planq lists the Bakkie seat as a molded shell made from dried coffee grounds and recycled plastic, on a powder-coated steel frame; the whole chair weighs 3.8 kilograms and stacks up to 20 high.
claims.source: PLANQ, "Bakkie," product page

claims.claim: Planq's four cards at its stand named the steps: coffee, dried coffee grounds, recycled plastic and coffee granulate. Card 03 said the plastic was post-industrial waste and card 04 said the blend becomes pellets molded into the shell.
claims.source: RN Collins, iPhone photo ip1741, Sunday 18 October 2026, Building TX; PLANQ, Bakkie collection page
claims.where: the four cards, read at full resolution

claims.claim: Planq's stand print and its collection page say "1 chair = 50 espressos". Planq gives no weight of grounds per shell and no share of grounds in the granulate.
claims.source: PLANQ, Bakkie collection page; RN Collins, iPhone photo ip1741

claims.claim: In one study of high-density polyethylene with 10 to 30 percent grounds by weight, adding the grounds made the material 49 percent stiffer but 21 percent weaker in tension.
claims.source: de Bomfim ASC et al., "Valorization of Spent Coffee Grounds as Precursors for Biopolymers and Composite Production," Polymers 14, no. 3 (2022): 437

claims.claim: Recycled polypropylene from espresso capsules filled with 20 and 30 percent espresso grounds had properties similar to virgin polypropylene; a coupling agent raised tensile strength by 18 percent and stiffness by 20 percent but lowered elongation and impact strength.
claims.source: de Bomfim ASC et al., Polymers 14, no. 3 (2022): 437
claims.study: one study, as described in a review

claims.claim: A 2025 study made a PHBV composite with 45 percent spent coffee grounds, ground and remolded it five times, and found stiffness up about 9.6 percent, tensile strength down 1.8 percent and elongation at break down about 18 percent.
claims.source: Janowski G et al., "Effect of Multiple Mechanical Recycling Cycles on the Structure and Properties of PHBV Biocomposites Filled with Spent Coffee Grounds (SCG)," Materials 18, no. 23 (2025): 5368

claims.claim: Espresso studies in a 2021 review used mostly 7 grams for a 25 milliliter shot up to 18.1 to 20.4 grams; on those ends, 50 espressos would use about 350 grams to 1 kilogram of ground coffee. That range is the piece's own calculation.
claims.source: Olechno E et al., "Influence of Various Factors on Caffeine Content in Coffee Brews," Foods 10, no. 6 (2021): 1208
claims.study: literature review; range calculated for this piece

claims.claim: A 2021 Dezeen Showroom listing, labeled partnership content, said the shell of Zuiver's Albert Kuip coffee chair contains 42.5 percent coffee waste and 57.5 percent polypropylene.
claims.source: Dezeen Showroom, "Albert Kuip Coffee chair by APE presented at Maison&Objet," 13 October 2021
claims.study: partnership listing, not an independent test

claims.claim: The V&A says Robin Day's polypropylene chair for Hille was introduced in 1963, and that a single tool could make 4,000 shells a week.

claims.claim: Directive (EU) 2024/825 bans a generic environmental claim without recognised excellent environmental performance, and a claim about the entire product when it concerns only one aspect of it.

could_be_wrong.point: The doctoral thesis on recycled coffee composites was read only as its two abstracts, because the full text is restricted.

The ranking of Coffee Based as one of the largest coffee waste processors comes from a listing that reads as the company's own promotion and gives no measure. The company's own site did not open.
The piece does not judge whether any Planq statement complies with EU or Dutch law on green claims. That is for regulators and courts.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, the wallet maker Secrid ran a talent podium that offered seven designers coaching and 7,777 euros each.
Secrid's own fund page and three impact reports show the money in and the money out, and the piece reads them line by line.
On the press tour, RN Collins filmed the co-founder's reason for the fund and one designer's minute, Bobby Kolade of Buzigahill.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every money figure was checked page by page against Secrid's own reports, but those are the company's own numbers: none gives a profit figure or says an outside accountant reviewed them. The quotes from the tour were checked word for word against the footage.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, people kept asking RN Collins whether she saw the work, and often she had not.
This piece opens a series that gives, for each work, how close she got by the time stamps on her own phone and camera files.
Then it says what each work was, from the makers' own pages, the festival programme and press kits.
start_here.how_sure_note: The times and what her frames show come from her own files and were checked. What each work was comes mostly from the makers' and festival's own pages, which were not tested, and a few matches are only likely.

summary: Dutch Design Week 2026 showed more ceramic work than RN Collins, a ceramicist, could reach in three days. Eight works never made it into her footage.
This piece tells each of the eight only from what its makers and the festival published: porcelain made new, clay that goes back to nature, and vessels used as tools.
It marks where a maker's claim had no public test behind it, and ends with the ceramics she did film: Atelier Fig.'s Fringe and Off World at Galerie Nasty Alice.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every fact about the eight works is what their makers and the festival published, read in full, and several of those claims have no public test behind them. The background, from a 1963 patent to a 2025 lacquer review, comes from original papers and official pages, with two read as abstracts only.

claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Porcelain Foam: experiment and potential," DDW26 programme page

claims.claim: A patent filed in 1961 and granted on 21 May 1963 describes coating an open-cell polyurethane foam pad in ceramic slurry and firing it to burn out the polyurethane.
claims.source: K. Schwartzwalder and A. V. Somers, "Method of making porous ceramic articles," US Patent 3,090,094, granted 21 May 1963

claims.claim: The filter claim, that the foam filters contaminants "down to microorganisms," was published with no test data.

claims.claim: JOYN's makers say the plates steer liquid toward the center and the extended rim gives places to grip, and that it was co-designed with people from an Alzheimer's center and care homes. No measured outcomes were published.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "JOYN: Inclusive Tableware," DDW26 programme page

claims.claim: Kalfa made casting bodies with 20% and 50% recycled sanitaryware. In her study, 92% would take the recycled cup home, acceptance fell to 33% for a kitchen countertop, and 58% would tell a guest where the cup came from.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Porcelain in Presence," DDW26 programme page
claims.study: perception study; sample size not published

claims.claim: Disclosure of origin shaped judgment more strongly than geometry or waste content.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week, "Porcelain in Presence," DDW26 programme page

claims.claim: Alveo is a 3D-printed clay reef module fired at 1050 degrees Celsius, with six design features copied from the honeycomb worm's reef. No field results were published.

claims.claim: There are descriptions of Sabellaria reefs in the Wadden Sea "that covered more than 100 hectares," and surveys in 2008 and 2015 found only a single worm.
claims.source: Wageningen University & Research, "A worm colony in the Wadden Sea," longread, 21 August 2025

claims.claim: A SCOBY is a biofilm of bacterial cellulose that "encapsulates a microbial community within it," and Xu shaped it by changing the openings of ceramic vessels.
claims.source: A. May, S. Narayanan, J. Alcock, A. Varsani, C. Maley and A. Aktipis, "Kombucha: a novel model system for cooperation and conflict in a complex multi-species microbial ecosystem," PeerJ 7:e7565, 2019; Dutch Design Week, "SCOBY Face," DDW26 programme page

claims.claim: Hitchcock wrote that lacquer "exudes from horizontal cuts in the bark" and put the most one tree gave at about 40 to 50 cubic centimeters.
claims.source: Romyn Hitchcock, "The preparation of Japanese lacquer and the manufacture of Wakasa lacquer ware," Proceedings of the United States National Museum, vol. 11, for 1888, pp. 473 to 479

claims.claim: Lacquer cures as the enzyme laccase links urushiol into a film, which needs 20 to 30 degrees Celsius and 70 to 80 percent humidity and can take weeks.

claims.claim: The lacquer tree carries urushiol, and most reactions are allergic contact dermatitis that appears 12 to 72 hours after contact.
claims.source: T. Lofgran, G. D. Mahabal and D. H. Schaffer, "Toxicodendron Toxicity," StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf NBK557866

glossary.plain: Liquid porcelain or clay. Porcelain Foam beat air straight into it, and Porcelain in Presence cast a new slip made partly from crushed toilets and sinks.
The usual way to make a ceramic foam: soak a polymer sponge in ceramic slurry, dry it, then fire it so the sponge burns away and leaves a ceramic copy.
Fired ceramic toilets and sinks. When a building is taken apart, they usually leave as crushed aggregate.
A reef of sand tubes built by the worm Sabellaria spinulosa. In the Dutch Wadden Sea only single worms are now found.
The symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast that forms when kombucha is brewed: a floating layer of bacterial cellulose with the microbes living inside it.
Japanese lacquer, made from the sap of the lacquer tree, which hardens in warm, damp air over weeks.
A highly allergenic oily resin found in the lacquer tree and in poison ivy, poison oak and poison sumac.
A delayed allergic skin reaction that appears 12 to 72 hours after contact, the most common reaction to urushiol.

safety.note: The raw sap of the lacquer tree carries urushiol, which can cause a delayed allergic skin reaction. That says nothing about finished lacquered pieces. Education, not medical advice.

summary: At Dutch Design Week 2026, Laura Civetti showed Adaptive System, a sleeveless top printed in 18 parts from maps of body curvature, heat and sun exposure.
Skin is not the same all over: thick skin on the palms and soles has a fifth layer, and in male athletes running hard the upper back sweated about ten times faster than the palms.
The top is a proof of concept built on simulated data, and no published source has tested it on a person. RN Collins did not see it in person.
start_here.how_sure_note: The skin and sweat facts come from an open textbook and peer-reviewed studies, though several of the sweat and sun studies could be read only as abstracts. What the top is and how it was made rests on the festival, the maker and the trade press, and no one has tested it on a wearer.

claims.claim: The press kit names three things that were mapped, body curvature, heat and solar exposure, and says they became three connected layers for movement, ventilation and protection.
claims.source: Dutch Design Week press kit 2408, "Adaptive system"

claims.claim: The top's structure was tuned to a color-coded map of simulated physiological data, and the report called it a demonstration of a design logic, not a finished product.
claims.source: Paloma Duran, "3D Printed Garment Is Built From Skin Data, Not a Size Chart," 3D Printing Industry, 27 July 2026

claims.claim: The top was printed on a Stratasys PolyJet 3D printer in 18 pieces, then assembled.
claims.source: All3DP, Carolyn Schwaar, "Fashion's Next Frontier Is 3D Printed, Data-Driven Second Skin," 2 June 2026, Internet Archive copy of 18 July 2026

claims.claim: Most skin is thin skin with four layers. Thick skin, found only on the palms and soles, has a fifth layer, the stratum lucidum.
claims.source: OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 5.1, "Layers of the Skin"

claims.claim: In male athletes at 75% of their maximal oxygen uptake, the center of the upper back sweated 1,197 grams per square meter per hour and the palms 119, about ten times less.
claims.source: Smith CJ, Havenith G, European Journal of Applied Physiology 111, no. 7 (2011): 1391 to 1404
claims.study: lab study of male athletes; abstract read; participant count not given in the abstract

claims.claim: Regional sweat rate did not track regional skin temperature and did not follow the known pattern of sweat gland density.
claims.source: Smith CJ, Havenith G, European Journal of Applied Physiology 111, no. 7 (2011): 1391 to 1404
claims.study: lab study of male athletes; abstract read

claims.claim: The palms and soles make up 5.2% of the body's surface but hold about a quarter of its sweat glands, yet each gland on the trunk puts out about 7 to 15 times more sweat.
claims.source: Taylor NAS, Machado-Moreira CA, Extreme Physiology & Medicine 2 (2013): 4
claims.where: gland density and sweat secretion sections

claims.claim: Of 4,063 Air Force flying personnel, none was near average on all ten measurements chosen as useful in clothing design.
claims.source: Gilbert S. Daniels, The "Average Man"?, Technical Note WCRD 53-7, US Air Force, December 1952
claims.study: analysis of the 1950 Air Force anthropometric survey

claims.claim: In body-mapped outfits, the design changed how warm 12 active men felt in 5 of 11 body regions, while overall thermal sensation and comfort stayed similar.
claims.source: Fournet D, Redortier B, Havenith G, Extreme Physiology & Medicine 4, suppl. 1 (2015): A74

idea-intersectionality-two-strikes.title: Two strikes at once: where 'intersectionality' came from

summary: In January 1974, layoffs by seniority at General Motors' St. Louis plant reached every Black woman in production, and five Black women sued for a class of all Black women.
In 1976 the trial judge said they could claim race discrimination or sex discrimination, "but not a combination of both"; in 1980 the Fifth Circuit read the same law the other way.
In 1989 Kimberlé Crenshaw used these cases to name the problem: intersectionality.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every quotation from the opinions, Crenshaw and Cooper was matched word for word with its source on November 23, 2026, so this is sure about what the papers say. It is not sure how the women's remaining race claim ended: no later published ruling was found.

could_be_wrong.point: How the women's race claim under Section 1981 ended is not known here. The appeals court returned it to the trial court in 1977, and no later published ruling was found; the searches were limited (one search service refused automated requests).

could_be_wrong.point: Crenshaw wrote that GM "simply did not hire Black women prior to 1964" and spoke of evidence at trial. The appeals court says GM employed one Black woman, a janitor, before 1970, and both opinions show the case was decided without a trial. The post follows the court's count.

The Jefferies court described the rejected "solely" amendment as modifying "sex." The House debate shows Representative Dowdy's amendment would have covered only discrimination "based solely on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin," not sex alone.
Jefferies note 7 cites the DeGraffenreid appeal as a Ninth Circuit case; the head matter of 558 F.2d 480 shows the Eighth Circuit decided it.
The larger Mosley case was not read. The one fact used about it, that its plaintiffs won part of their Title VII claim in 1980, rests on Crenshaw's note 10.
Courts did not agree. By 1980 two federal appeals courts had read the same statute in opposite ways, and even in Jefferies Judge Randall would have returned the question without deciding it.
The EEOC's 2006 guidance names intersectional discrimination, but the same page says its contents "do not have the force and effect of law."

idea-mkultra-1977-hearing.title: What the Senate learned about MKUltra in 1977

summary: In 1973 the CIA destroyed the files of MKUltra, its secret behavior program; in 1977 it found seven boxes of finance folders that had been filed in the wrong place.
A joint Senate hearing on August 3, 1977 put the find on the public page, with the Church Committee's report on testing without consent reprinted inside it.
Rules followed: Executive Order 12036 in 1978 required documented informed consent for intelligence research on people, and a 1978 law set up a presidential ethics commission.
start_here.how_sure_note: Every quotation was matched word for word with its source on November 23, 2026, so this is sure about what the papers say. Much stays unknown because the files were destroyed: asked how many people were recruited for the safehouse tests, Turner said "No idea."
